title: Connecting global policy and local knowledge to tackle the climate crisis
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/Simon.jpeg)

Political Science PhD student Simon Beaudoin explores how global cooperation can help address climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution\.

> Climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution are global challenges that no country can solve alone\. Yet efforts to address them are often fragmented across governments, institutions, and international agreements\.

[Simon Beaudoin](https://politics.ubc.ca/profile/simon-beaudoin/) studies how countries, institutions, and communities can work together more effectively on environmental challenges\. A PhD student in the UBC Department of Political Science, his research takes him from UN biodiversity negotiations to Pacific Island communities on the frontlines of climate change, searching for reforms that are both effective and just\.

He explores how local and Indigenous knowledge can inform international decision\-making, and how stronger cooperation can bridge the gaps between climate, biodiversity, and pollution policy\.

**What are you researching?**  
My research examines the relationship between governance and ecological systems and explores practical solutions to transboundary environmental issues\. I focus on three challenges: climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution — what the United Nations Environment Programme calls the “triple planetary crisis\.” By integrating insights from the social and natural sciences, I aim to identify more effective, inclusive, and cooperative responses to climate and environmental change\.

My doctoral fieldwork takes place in international environmental negotiations and in Pacific Island States, which are on the frontlines of climate change and environmental degradation while also leading global advocacy efforts related to climate, biodiversity, and pollution\.

For example, in Raja Ampat, an archipelago in Indonesia, I documented the work of Child Aid Papua, a non\-profit boarding school focused on ocean literacy and sustainability\. Located in one of the least educated regions in the world, the school hosts young people from the neighbouring islands and provides them with practical skills to become agents of change in their communities\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/dji_fly_20240517_172356_563_1715934608414_photo_optimized.jpg)

The Child Aid Papua school campus in Raja Ampat, West Papua, Indonesia\. The school is part of a community\-led initiative that combines education with environmental conservation\.

**Why have you chosen to devote your research to environmental issues?**  
The impacts of climate change reverberate across societies, species, ecosystems, and generations\. It is not only an environmental issue, but also a political, social, and ethical one that raises important questions of justice, sustainability, and peace\.

What particularly motivates me is the recognition that addressing shared environmental challenges can strengthen collective action and solidarity across borders\. I am also thinking of future generations, who I hope will have the immense pleasure of living on a healthy, resilient, and beautiful planet\.

“I hope my research encourages more integrated, long\-term, inclusive, and cooperative responses that recognize the fundamental interconnections between societies and the ecosystems they depend on\.”

Simon Beaudoin

PhD student, Department of Political Science

**You recently published a book on global biodiversity governance\. What is the book about, and why does this issue matter for people and the planet?**  
Biodiversity underpins many aspects of everyday life, including food systems, clean water, and climate stability\. My [book](https://www.puq.ca/catalogue/livres/gouvernance-mondiale-biodiversite-5008.html), co\-authored with Laura Fequino and Annie Chaloux, examines how global biodiversity governance has evolved over time, how political and economic decisions affect ecosystems and species, and how environmental change increasingly affects human health, economies and communities\. It also highlights opportunities for global biodiversity recovery and stronger international cooperation\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/IMG_8152.jpg)

Simon Beaudoin \(third from left\) at the Nagenahiru Foundation's environmental learning centre in Ambalangoda, Sri Lanka\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/P6021146-1.jpg)

Simon Beaudoin with Mentawai community members harvesting a sago palm in the Mentawai Islands, West Sumatra, Indonesia\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/dji_fly_20230605_154718_569_1686014198844_photo_optimized.jpg)

Lokal Lab’s Ihayas Farm in Siargao, Philippines\. Designed as a model for regenerative agriculture, the farm shows how nature\-based farming techniques can create affordable, profitable, and resilient food systems that can be replicated in other communities\.

**What’s one thing you’d like people to take away from your work?**  
Environmental issues cannot be addressed in isolation\. Environmental, political, economic, and social systems are deeply interconnected, and decisions made in one area often have far\-reaching consequences in another\. I hope my research encourages more integrated, long\-term, inclusive, and cooperative responses that recognize the fundamental interconnections between societies and the ecosystems they depend on\.

*Simon Beaudoin is a Pierre Elliott Trudeau Scholar, Killam Scholar, SSHRC Doctoral Fellow, and Fulbright Scholar \(Stanford University, 2025\)\. He is also the cofounder of [Possible](https://wepossible.org/), a non\-profit dedicated to social and ecological regeneration through education, research, and storytelling\.*

title: The hidden power of climate metaphors
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/markus-spiske-RXQhffGWPTQ-unsplash.jpg)

Poster from a global climate change strike in 2019\. \(Markus Spiske via Unsplash\)

> What role do metaphors play in how we understand the climate crisis, feel responsible for it, or become motivated to act on it?

When a politician says we’re “on a highway to climate hell,” a late\-night host compares climate change to “a car speeding off a cliff while some of us are fiddling with the radio,” or an activist poster shows a melting glacier in the shape of a drowning human, these framings do more than grab our attention\. They also nudge our brains toward specific emotions, assumptions, and ways of understanding the crisis\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/IMG-0040-740x1024-1.jpg)

Kimberly Grogan is a PhD candidate in the UBC Department of English Language and Literatures\.

[Kimberly Grogan](https://english.ubc.ca/profile/kim-grogan/) is a PhD candidate and cognitive linguist who studies the metaphors and images that shape how people make sense of the climate crisis\. Her research spans news media, television, and activist campaigns, exploring how different messages resonate with different audiences\.

In her [study](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397954084_%27Climate_cults%27_and_%27climate_sins%27_Religion_metaphors_and_the_framing_of_climate_change_in_American_and_Canadian_newspapers) of newspaper coverage in the US and Canada, she examined how religious metaphors — “climate cult,” “climate prophet,” “sacrificing prosperity on the altar of climate change” — are overwhelmingly used by conservatives to frame climate science as an irrational belief system\. She found that liberals, meanwhile, draw on concepts such as “sin” and “hell” to communicate the urgency of the crisis — sometimes reinforcing the very framing they seek to challenge\. She is now extending this research to activist campaigns by organizations like the WWF and Extinction Rebellion\.

A [Climate Storytelling Fellow](https://climatehope.sites.olt.ubc.ca/home-page/conference-programme/climate-storytelling-fellowship-ubc-students/), Grogan studies what makes climate messages persuasive — and how advocates can communicate more effectively with audiences beyond those already engaged in the issue\.

**How did you become interested in the use of metaphors in climate change communication?**

I’m originally from the United States, where there’s a lot of political polarization around climate change\. I became interested in following the different arguments for and against climate change’s validity, as I’ve always been very environmentally conscious\. I wanted to understand why certain climate change framing was ineffective, and how people who were arguing against the validity of climate change were doing so in a seemingly compelling manner\.

**What sources are you analyzing in your research?**

My dissertation examines metaphors in both textual and multimodal \(image\-text\) climate communication, with an eye towards the ways in which context, political affiliation, intent and belief shape what types of metaphors are deployed\.  I primarily analyze news periodicals and climate change activist campaigns\. I recently examined how religion metaphors are used by liberals and conservatives in America and Canada to frame climate change\. I’m currently working on documenting effective or ineffective metaphors that are used by the World Wildlife Fund and Extinction Rebellion\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/PHOTO-2026-05-28-15-24-35-1-1.jpg)

Kimberly Grogan presenting work on climate metaphors at the Cognitive Linguistics Conference of North America at UBC Okanagan\.

**What impact do you hope this research could have in addressing climate challenges?**

I hope my research and critique of public discourse and environmental campaigns about climate change can contribute to knowledge about how to create more effective climate change messaging that reaches and connects with a broader audience\. Because metaphor is so pervasive in climate change discourse, it has the ability to be a very powerful persuasive tool—if used well\.

**What’s the one thing you’d like people to take away from your work?**

Metaphor isn’t just a decorative literary device, and it can impact conceptualization and decision making about important public issues\! This is well known in cognitive linguistics, but less well\-known outside of the discipline\.

title: 13 Arts courses you can take to learn about Indigenous history and culture
content_markdown:

> Interested in learning how Indigenous histories, cultures, and communities shape the world around us? These courses explore Indigenous stories, resistance, creativity, and community—from right here on xʷməθkʷəy̓əm \(Musqueam\) territory to other Indigenous lands around the world\.

You’ll explore big topics like power, identity, and place, and come away with fresh perspectives on the world and your role within it\.

Below is a list of some of the Winter Session 2026/27 Arts courses you can take to learn more about Indigenous histories and cultures\. These courses are open to all Arts students without prerequisites, and many also fulfil the Place and Power credit requirement for [BA students who started in 2024/25 or later](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/#place-and-power)\.

***The course add/drop deadline for Winter Term 1 is Monday, September 21, 2026\.***

[Term 1 \(view 4 courses\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/13-arts-courses-you-can-take-to-learn-about-indigenous-history-and-culture-2026/#term-1-view-4-courses-34)

### **Indigenous Literature: NDN Time: Past and Presents Erased, Futures Foreclosed**

*ENGL\_V 373 \| Mon/Wed/Fri 3:00–4:00 PM*

Who gets to imagine the future, and who gets written out of it? This course explores Indigenous futurisms and speculative fiction, examining how Indigenous, Black, and racialized communities envision radical alternatives to mainstream narratives of what's to come\. You'll engage with Indigenous notions of time, kinship, and continuity as tools for imagining genuinely shared futures\.

What does it mean to read literature here, on unceded xʷməθkʷəy̓əm land? This course pairs works by Musqueam and local Indigenous authors with texts from elsewhere, asking how place, power, and the act of reading are always connected\. *Restricted to Creative Writing majors*

Taught by [Dr\. Billy\-Ray Belcourt](https://creativewriting.ubc.ca/profile/billy-ray-belcourt/)

Learn more about CRWR\_V 420X

*launch*

[Source link](https://creativewriting.ubc.ca/courses/?search=420X)

[Term 2 \(view 9 courses\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/13-arts-courses-you-can-take-to-learn-about-indigenous-history-and-culture-2026/#term-2-view-9-courses-35)

### **Arctic Art and Activism**

*CENS\_V 203, Sect\. 201 \| Tue/Thu 9:30–11:00 AM*

Indigenous peoples across the Arctic are facing unprecedented environmental and economic pressures from outside their communities\. This course explores neocolonialism in circumpolar regions, examining how Indigenous communities have fought to retain sovereignty over their lands and ways of life through collective action, art, and cultural revitalization\.

Taught by [Dr\. Tim Frandy](https://cenes.ubc.ca/profile/tim-frandy/)

Learn more about CENS\_V 203

*launch*

[Source link](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/courses/censv-203-arctic-art-and-activism)

---

### **Introduction to Creative Writing with an Indigenous Focus**

*CRWR\_V 220 \| Wed 12:00–2:00 PM*

Find your creative voice through an Indigenous lens\. This course introduces you to creative writing across three genres, from fiction and poetry to creative nonfiction, radio drama, and stage play, with Indigenous perspectives and storytelling at the centre\.

Taught by [Dr\. Billy\-Ray Belcourt](https://creativewriting.ubc.ca/profile/billy-ray-belcourt/)

Learn more about CRWR\_V 220

*launch*

[Source link](https://creativewriting.ubc.ca/courses/?search=220)

---

### **Introduction to Indigenous Studies**

*ENGL\_V 231 \| Mon/Wed/Fri 3:00–4:00 PM*

How long have Indigenous Peoples been making literature, and is literature only found in books? This course expands what it means to read and write, introducing you to Indigenous authors from North America and the Pacific through poetry, fiction, essays, oral storytelling, performance, film, and land\-based story\.

Taught by [Dr\. Alexa Manuel](https://english.ubc.ca/profile/alexa-manuel-2/)

Learn more about ENGL\_V 231

*launch*

[Source link](https://english.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=231)

---

### **Gender, Race and Indigeneity in Canada**

*GRSJ\_V 301 \| Tue/Thu 9:30–11:00 AM*

What do documented histories leave out, and what do narrated lives reveal? This course examines gender and Indigeneity through the recorded histories and lived experiences of Indigenous peoples in Canada, exploring how race, gender, and colonial structures have shaped and continue to shape Indigenous life\.

*Recommended for students who have completed GRSJ\_V 101 and GRSJ\_V 102, or have third\-year standing\.*

Learn more about GRSJ\_V 301

*launch*

[Source link](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/courses/grsjv-301-gender-race-and-indigeneity-canada)

---

### **Reading the Bible on Indigenous Lands**

*AMNE\_V 384 \| Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00–11:00 AM*

How were biblical texts used to justify European settler colonialism in North America? This course examines the reception and appropriation of the Bible on Turtle Island, with a focus on British Columbia, and traces the impact of Christianity on Indigenous communities through the Indian Act and Residential School system\.

Taught by [Dr\. Kurtis Peters](https://amne.ubc.ca/profile/kurtis-peters/)

Learn more about AMNE\_V 384

*launch*

[Source link](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/courses/amnev-384-reading-bible-indigenous-lands)

---

### **Topics in Place, Power, Poetics, and Narrative: Storying Indigenous Vancouver**

*ENGL\_V 376B \| Tue/Thu 11:00 AM–12:30 PM*

What does it mean to study literature on unceded xʷməθkʷəy̓əm land? This course foregrounds Musqueam teachings, stories, and relations alongside works by other Indigenous authors, exploring how literature and storytelling articulate identity, resurgence, and self\-determination\. You'll come away with a reshaped sense of what reading can be when approached through Indigenous ways of knowing\.

Taught by [Dr\. Dallas Hunt](https://english.ubc.ca/profile/dallas-hunt/)

Learn more about ENGL\_V 376B

*launch*

[Source link](https://english.ubc.ca/courses/)

---

### **Indigenous Latin America**

*LAST\_V 303 \| Tue/Thu 2:00–3:30 PM*

From the conquest to the present, this course surveys Indigenous cultures across Latin America, from the United States to Tierra del Fuego\. You'll explore a rich range of sources including chronicles, visual art, legal documents, novels, and oral history, drawing connections with the experience of Indigenous nations in Canada and critically examining concepts like decolonization and subalternity\.

Learn more about LAST\_V 303

*launch*

[Source link](https://las.arts.ubc.ca/last-303/)

---

### **Sámi Histories and Cultures**

*NORD\_V 340 \| Mon/Wed, 3:30 PM–5:00 PM*

Explore the diverse histories and cultures of Sámi people—the Indigenous Peoples of Norway, Sweden, Finland, and the Kola peninsula of Russia\. From reindeer to religion, from folklore to *Frozen II*, this course examines Sámi traditional culture, the impacts of settler colonialism upon it, and the ways revitalization and activism work as agents of decolonization today\.

Taught by [Dr\. Tim Frandy](https://cenes.ubc.ca/profile/tim-frandy/)

Learn more about NORD\_V 340

*launch*

[Source link](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/courses/nordv-340-sami-histories-and-cultures)

### **Indigenous Activism**

*NORD\_V 341 \| Tue/Thu, 3:30 PM–5:00 PM*

Indigenous communities in the circumpolar north are reshaping the political landscape through art, performance, and activism\. This course examines contemporary social and political conflicts across the Arctic region, exploring how First Peoples have mobilized creative and activist practices as powerful tools for resistance and decolonization\.

Taught by [Dr\. Tim Frandy](https://cenes.ubc.ca/profile/tim-frandy/)

Learn more about NORD\_V 340

title: Introduction to UBC Arts Undergraduate Journals
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/2026_UG-Journal_opt2.jpg)

> At UBC Arts, learning doesn’t stop at lectures, readings, or final papers\. It continues through student\-led publications and peer\-to\-peer collaborations with support from faculty\.

[What are the benefits?](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/intro-undergraduate-journals/#what-are-the-benefits-36)

Faculty of Arts undergraduate journals are built by students, for students\. They are spaces to experiment, question, and contribute, where your work can live beyond a single course and become part of a larger conversation\.

-   Deepen your research and strengthen your academic work\.
-   Refine your writing voice and develop a clear sense of audience and purpose\.
-   Build practical skills in collaboration, communication, and critical review through editorial or production roles\.
-   Connect with peers across disciplines, cultures, and perspectives\.
-   Contribute to ongoing conversations around community, identity, social impact, and more\.
-   Center voices and perspectives that might otherwise go unheard\.

---

### First Year Programs

#### The ONE

*The ONE* showcases writing from first\-year students participating in the [Arts One program](https://artsone.arts.ubc.ca/)\. The pieces published often blend literature, philosophy, and cultural analysis\. ONE showcases some of the best student work from the year, highlighting the original and sophisticated arguments that students have developed about the texts they have read in the courses\.  

Visit The ONE

*launch*

[Source link](https://artsone.arts.ubc.ca/publications/student-journal/)

#### The Capsule

Led by faculty and run by a student and alumni editorial team, *The Capsule* journal brings together work from across all five [Coordinated Arts Programs \(CAP\)](https://cap.arts.ubc.ca/) streams\. The result is a diverse, interdisciplinary glance of the ideas and research happening within the CAP community\.  

Visit The Capsule

*launch*

[Source link](https://blogs.ubc.ca/thecapsule/)

---

### Literature and Humanities

#### Beacon: UBC Journal of Media Studies

Beacon is an annual, student\-led multimedia journal featuring undergraduate work on media and technology from the [School of Journalism Writing and Media Studies](https://jwam.ubc.ca/)\. Peer\- and faculty\-reviewed, it brings together creative and academic pieces that explore media from fresh perspectives\. Students can submit up to four original works each year\.  

Visit Beacon

*launch*

[Source link](https://mediastudies.arts.ubc.ca/resources/opportunities/beacon-journal-of-media-studies/)

#### Cinephile

Cinephile is a graduate student\-edited, board\-reviewed journal from UBC’s Cinema and Media Studies program in the [Department of Theatre and Film](https://theatrefilm.ubc.ca/), publishing essays, research papers, and book reviews across film theory, history, criticism, and visual culture\. While focused on graduate\-level scholarship, undergraduate writing and film reviews may also be considered on merit\.  

Visit Cinephile

*launch*

[Source link](https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/cinephile)

#### Undergraduate Journal of Art History and Visual Culture

The Undergraduate Journal of Art History and Visual Culture highlights student research on art history, visual culture, and critical theory\. Published annually from the [Department of Art History and Visual Arts](https://ahva.ubc.ca/), it brings together work from across disciplines and provides a space for both scholarly and creative approaches to visual media\.  

Visit the AHVA journal

*launch*

[Source link](https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/UJAH)

#### UBC Journal of Historical Studies

The UBC Journal of Historical Studies is a student\-run publication featuring research exploring diverse historical topics and methodologies\. Supported by the [Department of History](https://history.ubc.ca/) and student associations, the journal is peer\- and faculty\-reviewed\. It publishes an annual issue each spring, with submissions collected in the fall and winter\.  

Visit the journal

*launch*

[Source link](https://www.ubcjhs.ca/)

#### UBC Journal of Philosophical Enquiries

The UBC Journal of Philosophical Enquiries features essays that explore philosophical questions, arguments, and traditions\. Showcasing standout undergraduate writing from across Canada, the journal is reviewed by faculty and edited by students—offering both a platform for strong scholarship and hands\-on publishing experience supported by the [Department of Philosophy](https://philosophy.ubc.ca/)\.  

Visit the journal

*launch*

[Source link](https://ubcjpe.wixsite.com/mysite)

---

### Social Sciences

#### The Journal of Political Studies

Published annually in partnership with the [Department of Political Science](https://politics.ubc.ca/), this journal features top student papers across areas like Canadian and U\.S\. politics, international relations, and political theory\. It is also a great way to gain hands\-on experience with academic publishing and peer review\.  

Visit the journal

*launch*

[Source link](https://jps.arts.ubc.ca/)

#### UBC Journal of International Affairs

The Journal of International Affairs \(JIA\) is UBC’s longest\-running undergraduate journal, established in 1985 by the [Department of International Relations](https://ir.arts.ubc.ca/)\.

Student\-run and internationally distributed, it publishes original research — spanning global security, trade, and development — selected through blind peer and faculty review\.  

Visit JIA

*launch*

[Source link](https://www.jiaubc.ca/)

#### Sojourners: Undergraduate Journal of Sociology

*Sojourners* is an undergraduate sociology journal from [UBC Department of Sociology](https://sociology.ubc.ca/), exploring social structures, inequalities, and lived experiences\. The first peer\- and faculty\-reviewed undergraduate sociology publication in North America, it showcases standout work from UBC students\.  

Visit Sojourners

*launch*

[Source link](https://sociology.ubc.ca/research/sojourners/)

#### Trail Six

Trail Six is a nationally recognized, student\-run journal supported by the [Department of Geography](https://geog.ubc.ca/)\. The Trail Six journal is open\-access and showcases a wide range of geography topics at the intersection of the natural and social sciences, supporting the global exchange of knowledge\.  

Visit Trail Six

*launch*

[Source link](https://trailsix.geog.ubc.ca/)

#### The IONA Journal of Economics

Published annually, The IONA Journal of Economics highlights outstanding student work and fosters dialogue between students and faculty at the [Vancouver School of Economics](https://economics.ubc.ca/)\. Its name reflects a tradition of scholarship and learning, inspired by both the UBC economics building and the historic Scottish island of Iona\.  

Visit The IONA Journal

*launch*

[Source link](https://www.ionajournal.ca/journal)

---

### Identity and regional studies

#### Augenblick

*Augenblick* is an undergraduate academic journal published by the UBC German Studies program within the [Department of Central, Eastern, and Northern European Studies](https://cenes.ubc.ca/)\. The journal offers students a platform to share their work and gain hands\-on publishing experience\. *Augenblick* is completed in consultation with German Studies faculty members\.  

Visit Augenblick

*launch*

[Source link](https://www.ubcaugenblick.com/)

#### Ignite: The Undergraduate Journal for GRSJ

*Ignite* showcases intersectional feminist scholarship from UBC students, publishing both academic and creative work exploring themes of feminism and systems of oppression, including racism, colonialism, sexism\. Supported by the [Institute for Gender, Race, Sexuality, and Social Justice](https://grsj.arts.ubc.ca/), *Ignite* provides an interdisciplinary platform for students to share critical, expressive work\.  

Visit Ignite

*launch*

[Source link](https://grsj.arts.ubc.ca/research/student-journals/)

#### LOGOS

*LOGOS* is a [Department of Ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern Studies](https://amne.ubc.ca/) undergraduate journal featuring student work on the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world\. It welcomes a range of submissions, from academic essays and translations to visual art and creative writing, offering different ways of engaging with ancient cultures and histories\.  

Visit LOGOS

*launch*

[Source link](https://amne-sa.arts.ubc.ca/logos/)

#### Tributaries

*Tributaries* is a multidisciplinary journal rooted in [UBC’s Asian Canadian and Asian Migration \(ACAM\)](https://acam.arts.ubc.ca/) studies program, exploring lived experiences, migration, identity, and community\. It publishes work from undergraduate and recent graduates across genres, from essays and poetry to visual and multimedia art\. The journal centres marginalized voices and supports submissions through an editorial revision process rather than peer review\.  

Visit Tributaries

*launch*

[Source link](https://acam.arts.ubc.ca/students/acam-student-journal/)

#### The Scanner

*The Scanner* is an undergraduate journal focused on Scandinavian and Nordic studies, publishing work across disciplines from history and literature to anthropology\. It features both academic and creative submissions, with opportunities to contribute as a writer or editor within a student\-led editorial process in consultation with faculty from the [Department of Central, Eastern, and Northern European Studies](https://cenes.ubc.ca/)\. This journal is run by the UBC Scandinavian and Nordic Student Association\.  

Visit The Scanner

*launch*

[Source link](https://ubcsnsa.weebly.com/scanner.html)

---

Whether you’re refining a research paper, experimenting with interdisciplinary thinking, or exploring questions of identity and culture, these journals reflect the breadth of inquiry across Arts\. Arts Undergraduate Journals showcase emerging voices, foster curiosity and critical engagement, and highlight the questions students are exploring as they take their learning further\.

Discover Arts Research

Explore the vast research within Arts and resources to support your work\.

**Learn more about our research**

[Source link](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/research/)

title: Six-Week StART: UBC Arts First-Year Transition Program
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2025/08/2025-First-Year-Bucket-List-Web_v3.jpg)

> Settling into university takes time, and that’s exactly what Six\-Week StART is for\.
> 
> Start strong with this free transition program that connects every new\-to\-UBC Arts student with an upper\-year Orientation Leader \(OL\)\. No sign\-up required\.

Think of your OL as your go\-to insider\. In the lead\-up to [Imagine UBC](https://students.ubc.ca/new-to-ubc/orientations/imagine-ubc/) and through mid\-October, they’ll check in with resources and involvement opportunities and answer your questions\.  

###### Why participate?

3,500\+

### new\-to\-Arts students

200\+

### Upper\-year Orientation Leaders

80%

### of students felt more connected to Arts

[What do I get out of a first\-year transition program?](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/six-week-start/#what-do-i-get-out-of-a-first-y-37)

**Automatic go\-to insider:** An upper\-year Arts student who’s been in your shoes will be with you every step of the way\. You can reply to their emails with questions, no matter how small\.

**Three check\-in emails:** Your Orientation Leader sends you bi\-weekly emails, each with a different focus\. Think of them as friendly touch points, not homework\.

**Arts\-specific resources:** Each email highlights real, useful information about academic advising, peer coaches, student clubs, and more\. All curated for you as a UBC Arts student\!

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/Imagine-UBC-Arts-5_web.jpg)

**Orientation Leader**

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/Imagine-UBC-Arts-8_web.jpg)

**Six\-Week StART participants**

Gathered for pizza along Main Mall

### What can I expect in the first six weeks?

#### Early September: Welcome and get involved

Your Orientation Leader introduces themselves and shares Arts involvement opportunities, including AUS and Compass\.

#### Late September: Academic resources

Take a focused look at Arts Academic Advising, Arts Peer Academic Coaches, and study support available to you\.

#### Mid\-October: Reflection

A check\-in as the first half of the term wraps up, with a chance to share your feedback about the program\.

[Questions everyone asks](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/six-week-start/#questions-everyone-asks-38)

**Do I need to sign up?**  
No\. All new UBC Arts students are automatically enrolled\. Just watch for your OL’s first email in early September\.

**Should I reply to check\-in emails?**  
Yes, please do\! Your OL is a real person who wants to hear from you\. Questions, thoughts, or a quick hello are welcome\. You can reply directly to any email they send\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/08/2026_BINGO-stack.png)

### Play Six\-Week StART BINGO until October 16

Complete activities across campus, from connecting with your OL in person to discovering your new favourite UBC Arts spot\. Play for a chance to win prizes, with a grand prize up for grabs\!

Winners will be contacted by email in **late October 2026**\.

[How it works in 5 steps](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/six-week-start/#how-it-works-in-5-steps-39)

**1\.** Complete five squares in any row, column, or diagonal to get a BINGO\.

**2\.** For each square, do the activity described\. Mark it off with signed initials \(when prompted\) or get it stamped by a staff member\.

**3\.** How far can you go?

-   BINGO — complete any 1 line of 5 → prize draw entry
-   BINGO Bonus — complete any 2 lines of 5 → bonus prize draw entry
-   Purple Out — complete all 25 squares → grand prize draw entry

**4\.** Got BINGO, a BINGO Bonus, or a Purple Out? Fill in your name, student ID, and contact information on the card to be entered for a prize draw\.

**5\.** Drop your card into a prize draw box at the Compass Student Engagement Hub in Brock Commons South, Level 3\.

You don’t need to do everything in order, and you don’t need to do it perfectly\. The point is to get out there, try something new, and make UBC feel a little more like home\.

**Didn’t get a BINGO card in your welcome tote?** No worries\. Extras are available at the Arts Undergraduate Society office at the [Arts Student Centre](https://maps.app.goo.gl/VmRoG5iaafVAe9SF7) or at the Arts Co\-op front desk in [Brock Commons South, Level 3](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ksaaPDjN3L2vfJ716)\.

---

title: It’s just a game — so why do we care so much?
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/2026-AC-FootballEditorial-v1.2.jpg)

Header image by Jacob Pryce, ASC Communications

> When 52,000 people filled BC Place to watch Canada’s men’s soccer team face Qatar, strangers embraced and high\-fived, the roar of the crowd grew louder with every goal, and people who had never particularly followed the sport found themselves on their feet screaming, cheering, and swept up in the excitement\.

That intense, communal, and often difficult\-to\-explain feeling happens at every major sporting event and extends well beyond sport—from Swifties singing in unison at a concert to protestors marching shoulder to shoulder\.

What drives these emotional experiences in large crowds, and why do sporting outcomes feel so personal to those watching from the stands?

We spoke with three UBC Arts researchers to understand the forces behind fandom and the emotions that come with being a supporter\. They argue that the answer has less to do with sport itself and more to do with how humans build identity, attachment, and belonging through shared experience\.

---

### **How a team becomes your team**

[Dr\. Neil Armitage](https://sociology.ubc.ca/profile/neil-armitage/), a UBC sociologist who researched football spectatorship in his postgraduate studies, argues that fandom begins earlier than most people realize and less consciously than they might think\. Many lifelong fans do not initially fall in love with the sport itself, but with the experience surrounding it\. “As a child, you’re not going to a stadium alone,” he explains\. “You’re going with a parent or someone close to you, and there’s already an emotional connection there\. That bond then becomes associated with the experience of the game\.”

As children are gradually introduced to the crowd, Armitage explains, it can begin to take on some of the characteristics of what sociologists call a primary group—the close\-knit groups, like family and peers, through which we first form our sense of who we are\. Because this happens during childhood, the attachment forms at a foundational level\. “That’s where the ‘we’ comes from,” he says\. “There’s no separation between you and the team, because you are the team, and the team is you\.”

[Dr\. Jessica Tracy](https://psych.ubc.ca/profile/jessica-tracy/), a UBC professor of psychology whose research focuses on self\-conscious emotions like pride and shame, explains what that attachment looks like psychologically: “As humans, we tie our sense of self to much larger entities,” she says\. “There’s what we call a collective self, which is your identity at a much broader level\. One of the groups that become really easily tied up in people’s sense of collective self are teams that represent communities such as your university, state, or country\.”

### **The rituals of fandom**

Once fandom takes hold, it is the rituals that reinforce it, and sport offers plenty of them\. Armitage argues that rituals are the mechanism through which fan identity gets reinforced over time and that they’re learned, not instinctive\. “It’s not something you just pick up; it’s something you learn, something you become part of,” he says\. The jerseys, chants, pre\-match routines, familiar songs, and recurring traditions all help transform fandom from a casual interest into something deeper\.

Just as importantly, these rituals connect people to one another\. Over time, fans begin to recognize the same people in the stands — people they see every week, whose names they may not know, and with whom conversation rarely strays beyond the latest signing, injury, or result\. “You don’t meet them for drinks, you don’t see them anywhere else,” Armitage says\. “They’re not friends in the conventional sense, but their presence matters, and over time, these familiar faces become part of the ritual itself\.”

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/Fandom3-1.jpg)

Supporters make their way to BC Place ahead of Canada's match against Qatar\. Shared rituals—from wearing team colours to singing anthems and gathering before kickoff—help reinforce fan identity and belonging\. Photo: Alycia S, ASC Communications

“There's no separation between you and the team, because you are the team, and the team is you\.”

Dr\. Neil Armitage

Lecturer, Department of Sociology

---

### **Once a fan, always a fan?**

That sense of fan identity tends to be long\-lasting\. [Dr\. Friedrich Götz](https://psych.ubc.ca/profile/friedrich-gotz/), a UBC personality psychologist who has spent years studying how fans experience major tournaments including [two FIFA World Cups](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00497/full), recognizes this pull in his own life\. A lifelong soccer fan who grew up in Germany, his connection to the sport has faded with physical distance and time, but the World Cup arriving on his doorstep has pulled something back\. “It’s easy to reconnect to that former version of myself and get swept away by the fun of it all,” he says\.

Tracy’s research suggests why\. “If part of your identity is ‘I am a Canucks fan,’ that is part of your identity even when it’s not hockey season,” she says\. “It’s maybe a little dormant, but it’s still there—just like a parent is a parent no matter what, even when their kids have grown up and moved away\.”

### **The emotional cost of caring**

But what about when a team is struggling? When losses pile up, does that attachment start to fade?

Research would suggest it should\. Götz points to the work of the late Nobel laureate and former UBC professor Dr\. Daniel Kahneman, who argued that humans are generally more sensitive to losses than gains\. “Sport does not seem to be an exception to this pattern\. That said, some losses sting more than others and some victories mean more than others,” he says\.

Tracy offers the evolutionary context\. “Bad is stronger than good, which is kind of the way psychologists talk about it,” she says\. “When we feel bad, that’s a really important signal that we need to change our behaviour, often to survive\. That’s why the negative often feels bigger than the positive\. We evolved to really respond intensely to those negative signals\.”

It’s not just losing that hurts, Tracy adds, but losing when you expected to win\. “A team that loses year after year — it’s not fun, it certainly doesn’t evoke any pride, but it’s not as horribly shaming as it is to lose the big game that you really expected to win,” she adds\.

And yet fans return, season after season\. Tracy points to the community that forms around shared experience, including shared suffering\. “It makes us feel part of our environment and less alone,” she says\. “There’s probably solidarity with other fans who are going through the same thing\.”

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/Soccer-stadium.jpg)

Canadian and Qatari supporters fill BC Place during the 2026 FIFA World Cup\. For many supporters, the crowd itself is part of the appeal, offering a chance to be part of something larger than oneself\. Photo: Alycia S, ASC Communications

“Even if you didn’t enter the stadium as a die\-hard team Canada fan, celebrating six goals alongside thousands of others is a major bonding experience that makes us feel connected to each other and something bigger than ourselves\.”

Dr\. Friedrich Götz

Associate Professor, Department of Psychology

---

### **The power of the crowd**

Part of what draws fans back, Armitage suggests, is what the crowd itself offers, something perhaps seen most clearly during global tournaments like the FIFA World Cup\. “In the modern world, where we’re expected to be always on show and promoting ourselves, it’s great to be able to go somewhere and just be part of something,” he says\. “The rituals before, during, and after the game allow you to escape the pressures of modern life and exist as part of a group without having to perform\.”

Armitage knows this feeling firsthand\. Attending a Champions League match—not as a fan of either team, but as a researcher—he found himself swept up anyway\. “The anthem comes on, everyone stands up, so what do you do? You stand up\. And then the music kicks in, and you lose yourself,” he recalls\. “You become part of a psychological crowd\. The contagion is there — you feel it\.”

For a few hours, life becomes something simpler\. “It just becomes us versus them, home versus away, your colour versus theirs,” Armitage says\. He likens the stadium to theatre, but unscripted: “You have a play on the stage that’s unwritten\. You have rules, but you don’t know the outcome\. The players come from the same origins as the crowd; they emerge from the chorus onto the main stage, and the crowd remains as the chorus, interpreting everything in real time\. When a goal happens, or a penalty is awarded, or someone is sent off — all three stages, the pitch and the two sets of fans, coalesce and pandemonium sets off\.”

That reaction is made possible, Armitage explains, by something the crowd uniquely offers: anonymity\. “You can be absorbed into something larger, which is when emotional contagion happens,” he says\. “This is your steam valve of society and where people let things off\. It’s a cathartic experience\.”

Tracy’s research confirms the mechanism\. “When you’re with people who feel a certain emotion, you are more likely to start feeling that emotion\. It is literally contagious,” she adds\.

[Studying German fans during the 2018 World Cup](https://online.ucpress.edu/collabra/article/6/1/15/113063/What-Drives-Our-Emotions-When-We-Watch-Sporting), Götz found that while strongly identified fans responded most intensely to results, the crowd itself had an independent pull\. “Everybody feels something\. Even non\-fans tend to get drawn in,” he says\.

### **More than a game**

Armitage is clear that sport is simply the most visible expression of a much broader human behaviour\. The same dynamic—collective identity formed through shared ritual and emotional experience—plays out at concerts, in religious services, fan clubs built around artists, or shared passions\. “It’s the same mechanism at play, just a slightly different arena,” he says\.

Götz saw this at a national scale during the 2006 World Cup in Germany when the team’s success created a wave of shared national pride\. “It was a moment that transcended all societal strata and united people, whether they had previously cared about soccer or not,” he says\. “In a way, it redefined many Germans’ relationship with their country\.”

He sees the early signs of something similar taking shape in Vancouver\. Canada’s men’s national team is in the tournament, they are scoring goals, and people who have never watched soccer are paying attention\. “This builds a social and cultural momentum that soccer rarely achieves in our hockey\-dominated society,” Götz adds\. ​​“Even if you didn’t enter the stadium as a die\-hard team Canada fan, celebrating six goals alongside thousands of others is a major bonding experience that makes us feel connected to each other and something bigger than ourselves\.”

title: Arts in the Media: June 2026
content_markdown:
> [Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2020/01/About-Banner-Buchanan-Courtyard-UBC-Arts.jpg)
> 
> This month, UBC Arts faculty were featured in media outlets including *CBC, Global News, The Conversation*, and the *South China Morning Post*\. Their expertise informed reporting on topics including Canadian politics, climate and energy policy, AI and online safety regulation, and loneliness, well\-being, and social connection\.

---

### **Center for the Study of Democratic Institutions** 

**The Conservative Party recently released an AI\-generated ad\. How do voters feel about this kind of content?  
**Dr\. Chris Tenove said it would be preferable for all political parties to label AI\-generated content, but noted it is still an open question whether such a requirement should be mandatory given potential enforcement challenges\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/conservative-ai-ad-targets-carney-9.7240936)

---

### **Department of Arts History, Visual Art & Theory**

**Artist behind controversial photograph in Fredericton gallery defends it as ‘sacred’  
**Professor Christine D’Onofrio said the work originally related to the AIDS epidemic and changes meaning over time depending on the viewer\.  
[Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11918246/andres-serrano-piss-christ-controversy-fredericton-gallery/)

---

### **Department of Geography**

**Apartments can become sweltering in summer\. Why heat bylaws could be coming to a city near you  
**Dr\. Mohammed Rafi Arefin said there is significant research to suggest that when environmental regulations are adopted, tenants often bear the costs — unless there is another source of funding\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/whatonearth/heat-bylaws-climate-change-9.7250910)

**How to live in a restless world  
**Dr\. Michele Koppes said accepting uncertainty about climate change can help people cope with grief and anxiety, noting that “control is a fallacy” and resilience comes from adapting to ongoing change\.  
[The Narwhal](https://www.thespec.com/news/canada/how-to-live-in-a-restless-world/article_80ac8d0f-96e4-52b2-9016-a02c133e834b.html) \(paywall\)

**How Taiwan is balancing between American and Chinese visions of energy dominance  
**Dr\. Philippe Le Billon argues that U\.S\. “energy dominance” is proving limited, as global energy control remains fragmented while China advances in clean energy and import\-dependent states like Taiwan face growing security risks\.  
[The Conversation](https://theconversation.com/how-taiwan-is-balancing-between-american-and-chinese-visions-of-energy-dominance-284701)

**Ex\-member of top climate body says Alberta pipeline deal is not compatible with net\-zero  
**Dr\. Simon Donner, a former co\-chair of Canada’s Net\-Zero Advisory Body, said the federal pipeline deal with Alberta is not compatible with Canada’s 2050 net\-zero target, arguing that governments should be transparent with Canadians about the emissions implications of approving such projects\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/net-zero-advisory-body-9.7229357)

---

### **Department of History**

**When going to ‘camp’ meant Roman military lodgings — not summer fun  
**Dr\. Leslie Paris discussed how summer camps evolved from programs aimed at building leadership and resilience in boys into spaces that shaped childhood, community and American identity\.  
[NPR News](https://www.ideastream.org/npr-news/2026-06-25/when-going-to-camp-meant-roman-military-lodgings-not-summer-fun)

**The ‘Woodstock’ of housing conferences was held in Vancouver 50 years ago\. Why was it forgotten?  
**Dr\. Eagle Glassheim said Vancouver’s 1976 Habitat Forum highlighted experimental housing and renewable energy ideas, including low\-cost recycled\-material shelters, early electric vehicles, and broader solutions for housing and infrastructure challenges linked to global urbanization\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/retrospective-habitat-i-un-conference-vancouver-1976-9.7228633)

---

### **Department of Linguistics**

**Scientists reveal why David Attenborough’s voice makes him the perfect narrator  
**Dr\. Molly Babel says David Attenborough’s voice is perceived as especially pleasant due to the way his vocal folds vibrate, shaping its acoustic quality\.  
[Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.com/sciencetech/article-15792007/David-Attenborough-VOICE-Scientists-reveal.html)

---

### **Department of Political Science**

**Findlay needs a seat: Conservatives weigh potential by\-election options  
**Dr\. Stewart Prest said new B\.C\. Conservative leader Kerry\-Lynne Findlay faces delicate political and strategic decisions as she seeks a seat in the legislature\.  
[Times Colonist](https://www.timescolonist.com/local-news/findlay-needs-a-seat-conservatives-weigh-potential-byelection-options-12482285)

**David Eby leaving for trade mission to China but will fly home a few days early  
**Dr\. Kathryn Harrison said Ottawa is seeking B\.C\.’s support while the province looks to secure concessions in negotiations with the federal government\.  
[Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11940978/david-eby-trade-mission-china-fly-home-early/)

**Will B\.C\. Conservatives’ new leader build a big tent or forge new rightward direction?  
**Dr\. Stewart Prest said he expects the next few years in B\.C\. politics to be “bruising and quite divisive,” adding that he is concerned debates will become overly simplistic rather than nuanced\.  
[The Province](https://theprovince.com/news/will-bc-conservatives-new-leader-build-big-tent-or-forge-rightward-direction/wcm/5a415b17-edde-4650-8e31-077e2d41dbb5)

**Hanoi provides platform for Thai, Cambodian PMs to voice commitment to peace  
**Dr\. Yves Tiberghien said the ASEAN Future Forum showed how the region provides a rare platform for sustained dialogue between leaders, with both prime ministers offering cooperative and peace\-oriented messages that reflect shared interests and ASEAN’s role in fostering long\-term regional stability\.  
[Tuo Itre News](https://news.tuoitre.vn/hanoi-provides-platform-for-thai-cambodian-pms-to-voice-commitment-to-peace-103260610173055867.htm)

**How to rebuild what the great powers broke  
**Dr\. Yves Tiberghien argues that global “rupture” and multipolarity are enabling middle powers to reshape international order through cross\-regional coalitions that mediate great\-power rivalry and support more stable, decentralized global governance\.  
[East Asia Forum](https://eastasiaforum.org/2026/06/02/how-to-rebuild-what-the-great-powers-broke/)

---

### **Department of Psychology**

**An ordinary mind on an ordinary day  
**Dr\. Kalina Christoff discussed how spontaneous thought and mind\-wandering can foster creativity and insight\.  
[Lapham’s Quarterly](https://www.laphamsquarterly.org/roundtable/ordinary-mind-ordinary-day)

**Is BC’s new disability funding putting some kids at risk?  
**Dr\. Connor Kerns said many autistic children experience co\-occurring mental health conditions, emphasizing the importance of timely access to appropriate supports\.  
[The Tyee](https://thetyee.ca/News/2026/06/29/BC-New-Disability-Funding-Kids-Risk/)

**Chatbots are like potato chips: Understanding loneliness in the digital age  
**Dr\. Elizabeth Dunn’s research suggests AI chatbots may offer short\-term support but should not replace human connection, as relying on them for companionship could increase feelings of emotional loneliness over time\.  
[Association for Psychological Science](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/observer/chatbots-potato-chips.html)

**Canada introduces safe social media act to protect children  
**Dr\. Amori Mikami said questions remain about how Canada’s new online harms legislation will be implemented, including whether required safeguards will effectively protect young people from harmful online content\.  
[Medscape News Canada](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/canada-introduces-safe-social-media-act-protect-children-2026a1000lj9?form=fpf)

**Laughing amidst the gloom: How activists embrace joy in the fight to save Earth  
**Dr\. Jiaying Zhao said joy may have evolutionary roots in survival, noting that rewarding positive emotions can reinforce behaviour and spread socially through “contagion,” encouraging others to participate\.  
[The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/lifestyle/living/2026/06/01/laughing-amidst-the-gloom-how-activists-embrace-joy-in-the-fight-to-save-earth)

---

### **Department of Sociology**

**World Cup delivers double dose of patriotism for Canadian dual citizens  
**Dr\. Neil Armitage said the FIFA World Cup has given Canadians an opportunity to express a distinctive, inclusive form of nationalism, with the tournament fostering patriotism through shared support, fairness, and community\.  
[CTV News](https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/world-cup-delivers-double-dose-of-patriotism-for-canadian-dual-citizens/)

**B\.C\. must learn from Site C dam before starting new projects, says environmentalist  
**Dr\. David Tindall said major projects like Site C face strong public scrutiny over cost and environmental impact, but recent geopolitical tensions have also shifted some opinion toward greater support for new energy infrastructure\.  
[Vancouver is Awesome](https://www.vancouverisawesome.com/national-news/bc-must-learn-from-site-c-dam-before-starting-new-projects-says-environmentalist-12429999)

---

### **School of Public Policy and Global Affairs**

**‘Dangerous moment’: academic calls for US expulsion from WTO over protectionism  
**Dr\. Kristen Hopewell said rising protectionism is undermining the WTO and argued that allowing the U\.S\. to remain despite violating trade rules weakens the rules\-based system and encourages similar behaviour by other countries\.  
[South China Morning Post](https://www.scmp.com/economy/global-economy/article/3358225/dangerous-moment-academic-calls-us-expulsion-wto-over-protectionism)

**Canada’s social media ban for kids may narrow\. Experts say that’s good  
**Dr\. Heidi Tworek \(History and School of Public Policy and Global Affairs\) said the bill pairs restrictions with incentives for platforms to improve safety features while still recognizing that social media can offer educational and social benefits for some young users\.  
[Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11900484/social-media-online-harms-age-restriction-enforcement-questions/)

---

### **Vancouver School of Economics**

**What happens to CUSMA on July 1? The paths ahead as review set to begin**  
Dr\. Michael Devereux said Canada, the U\.S\., and Mexico are likely to continue negotiating changes to CUSMA beyond the July 1 review, stressing that businesses need greater certainty and that terminating the agreement would be highly damaging to all three economies\.  
[Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11942931/cusma-review-july-1-explained/)

**BMO branch closure brings anxiety for some seniors in Prince Rupert, B\.C\.  
**Dr\. Michael Devereaux said banks face rising costs in maintaining physical branches, including staffing and real estate expenses driven up by urban property booms\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bmo-branch-closure-prince-rupert-9.7240953)

**Canada keeps slipping in world happiness rankings\. Why are we so sad?  
**Dr\. John Helliwell said young Canadians are experiencing lower well\-being, highlighting the role of social connection and trust in improving happiness\.  
[Yahoo News](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/canada-keeps-slipping-in-world-happiness-rankings-why-are-we-so-sad-133915259.html)

---

Arts in the Media

Every month, Arts faculty share their expertise with media outlets on a variety of topics\.

**View previous instalments**

title: New books by Arts faculty for your 2026 reading list
content_markdown:
> [Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/06/New-books-2026.png)
> 
> This year, UBC Arts scholars have published books covering a fascinating range of topics — from a 300\-year linguistic cover\-up in Austria and the deskilling of immigrant professionals in Canada, to a rescue dog who saves a struggling vet student, the cognitive science of internet memes, and a dystopian world where memory itself is currency\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Ana-P.png)

### **[Tùgûl̈ “Txì xtěn rǎ gǎmy” ‘The celebration of the Day of the Dead: “The day of the souls”’](https://sites.google.com/view/tugul/inicio)**

By: [Ana Laura Arrieta\-Zamudio](https://linguistics.ubc.ca/profile/ana-laura-arrieta-zamudio/), PhD Candidate, Department of Linguistics

**What is your book about?**

This is the first graphic novel written entirely in San Pablo Güilá Zapotec \(Spanish and English versions are also available\)\. It follows Juana \(Xwân\), José \(Sê\), and their children Dulce \(Nàx\) and Pedro \(Bêd\) as they prepare to celebrate the Day of the Dead in San Pablo Güilá\. It also focuses on modals \(that is, expressions about notions like possibility and necessity, like English ‘must’, ‘might’\) in San Pablo Güilá Zapotec\. The Day of the Dead is a major holiday in Mexico, and communities celebrate it in different ways\. This book provides insight into how it is celebrated in San Pablo Güilá \(a Zapotecan community in Oaxaca, Mexico\)\. It also allows other linguists interested in modals to see how they are expressed in this language\.

**Why did you write this book?**

This book is the result of my PSI grant\. It is a community\-based collaboration\. The co\-authors of the story, who are also members of the community and native speakers of San Pablo Güilá Zapotec, are Dulce Rocío Santiago Morales, Ana Mey Maricela Morales Cruz, and Virginia Morales Cruz\. The illustrations were made by the Zapotecan artist José Froylan López García and graphic designer Sergio Tamayo Castelar\. This book will serve as a useful resource for language documentation and a tool for language revitalization, since printed copies were distributed to local teachers, and the three versions are available to the general public for free in digital form\. This book combines community work with material design for linguists interested in modals, while also showcasing an important celebration\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/08/Ana-Vivaldi.png)

### **[Urban Indigenous Assemblages: Qom Mobilities and the Remaking of White Buenos Aires](https://www.vanderbiltuniversitypress.com/9780826508386/urban-indigenous-assemblages/)**

By: [Dr\. Ana Vivaldi](https://sociology.ubc.ca/profile/ana-vivaldi/), Sessional Lecturer, Departments of Sociology and Department of Anthropology

**What is this book about?**

*Urban Indigenous Assemblages* explores how Qom people navigate racialization in the city, remake urban space and Indigenous life in Buenos Aires\. In a city long imagined by Argentina’s elites as white and European, Qom people are simultaneously recognized as Indigenous and racialized as part of the non\-white urban poor\. Based on 18 months of ethnographic research, the book follows the movements that connect a Qom barrio in Greater Buenos Aires with rural communities in the Chaco, other Indigenous urban spaces, city institutions, and the city centre\. These mobilities create forms of Indigenous territoriality that extend beyond bounded places and conventional ideas of indigeneity\. Through the concept of Indigenous assemblages, the book examines how everyday practices, movements, and relationships produce Indigenous spaces while challenging the racial and spatial boundaries through which Buenos Aires has been imagined\. The book thus rethinks urban Indigenous life through mobility, race, and the remaking of territory\.

**Why did you write this book?**

I wrote this book out of a sense of the invisibility of Indigenous and non\-white people in Buenos Aires, the city where I grew up and lived for half of my life\. I was also struck by the fact that researchers working with Indigenous people generally travelled far from the city, to rural communities\. I wanted to challenge this separation between rural and urban and to unpack the unspoken and largely unrecognized racism embedded in the making of Buenos Aires as a supposedly race\-less city and society\.

I became particularly interested in Qom’s people movement, against the idea that Indigenous people are fixed in place and bounded within the territories the state recognizes as Indigenous\. I wanted to understand the connections between Indigenous people, rural\-to\-urban migrants, and wider histories of mass political mobilization, including Peronism and unionism\. Ultimately, the book asks us to see Indigenous people not as “ethnic minorities” at the margins of the city, but as key political actors who reshape space and create an Indigenous territoriality that exceeds the boundaries imposed by the state\.

Attend a roundtable event on October 8, 2026

*launch*

[Source link](https://rdm.ubc.ca/events/post-nationhood-belonging-and-exclusion-latin-american-studies-roundtable)

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Ben-Bryce.png)

### [**Grounds for Exclusion: Race, Health, and Disability in Argentine Immigration Policy, 1876\-1932**](https://uncpress.org/9781469695358/grounds-for-exclusion/)

By: [Dr\. Benjamin Bryce](https://history.ubc.ca/profile/benjamin-bryce/), Associate Professor, Department of History

**What is this book about?**

I stumbled into this project, but the more I dug the more I realized it was an important story that needed to be told\. Argentina’s immigration story has mostly focused on community histories of the six million Europeans who arrived between the 1870s and 1930\. When I came across a diplomatic row in 1912 between Argentine and British officials about 600 Punjabi immigrants, something felt very off\. If that incident could vanish so completely from national memory and the stories that historians and museums tell, I wanted to know what else had been left out\. The answer turned out to be a great deal\. Once I started looking for the machinery of exclusion, I found it everywhere — in health inspections, in the work of consuls in Europe and Asia, in small clauses in immigration law, in the quiet refusals at ports of departure that never generated the kind of paper trail that arrivals do\.

**Why did you write this book?**

I also wrote it because Argentina’s “nation of immigrants” story isn’t unique\. Canada and the United States have built self\-images around the arrival of millions of people while saying much less about the mechanisms that decided who counted as desirable and who they excluded\. As I argue in the book, the widespread inclusion of millions of people in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries – in Argentina and other settler societies – was predicated on the exclusion of others\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Joy-Dixon.png)

### [**Sexual Heresies: Religion, Science, and Sexuality in Modern Britain**](https://www.sup.org/books/history/sexual-heresies)

By: [Dr\. Joy Dixon](https://history.ubc.ca/profile/joy-dixon/), Associate Professor, Department of History

**What is your book about?**

*Sexual Heresies* explores the ways that, in Britain at the turn of the last century, the new sexual sciences—from an anthropology that located the roots of religion in ancient fertility cults to psychoanalytic theories that explained religious experience in terms of psychosexual development—characterized religion as closely connected to or as a displacement of the sexual\. Those changing understandings of sexuality also transformed what was meant by “religion” and created a new concern with differentiating “normal” from “abnormal” forms of religiosity\. The book then goes on to track the impact of and response to that move across multiple sites: in liberal modernist theology in both the Catholic and Anglican churches, in occult or esoteric religions and “sexual magic,” among Anglican evangelicals and Anglo\-Catholics, and in secularist free\-love and free\-thought and “pagan” anti\-clericalism\. I argue that the increasing concern to police “sexual heresies” led to a narrowing of sexual possibilities inside “orthodox” religion and the association of alternative forms of religion with dissident sexualities that continues to shape both religion and secularism today\.

**Why did you write this book?**

Histories of religion and sexuality are often written as though they had nothing to do with each other, or as though they are always somehow in opposition to each other \(for example, in the idea that religion is inevitably sexually oppressive, and that sexual liberation is inherently secular\)\. I wanted to tell a more complicated story that does justice to the diversity of responses to changing ideas about sexuality from a variety of perspectives and traditions\. The book is, in the end, an effort to track the creative ways that people have found to make sense of the relationships between faith \(or its absence\) and desire in their own lives, and to clarify some of what is at stake in that process\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Katherine-B.png)

### **[The Oxford Handbook of Global Realisms](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/56841)**

By: [Dr\. Katherine Bowers](https://cenes.ubc.ca/profile/katherine-bowers/), Associate Professor, Department of Central, Eastern and Northern European Studies

**What is this book about?**

Realism is an artistic practice that aims to faithfully represent reality\. Historically, it has been practiced across different media, from early pictorial art and epic oral narratives, through literature and visual arts, to film, music, and digital media\. By foregrounding diverse theories, practices, and forms of realism, this volume revises the Eurocentric geography of the concept\. It offers a broad chronology that overcomes the fixation in studies of realism on the nineteenth century as its starting point and offers, instead, a more flexible timeline of this artistic practice\. The handbook presents realism as a transnational, transhistorical, and intermedial global phenomenon\.

**Why did you write this book?**

We wanted to understand why our field’s conceptualization and historicization of realism seemed so different from that of other disciplines\. As we began to research this, we were struck by the diversity of realisms across different literatures, cinemas, and art forms, and the lack of resources that attempted to speak to this diversity as a whole\. *The Oxford Handbook of Global Realisms*, co\-edited with Dr\. Margarita Vaysman \(University of Oxford\), emerged from this line of inquiry and the conversations we had with colleagues across disciplinary lines\.

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Max-C.png)

### **[Divided We Fall](https://formaclorimerbooks.ca/contributor/max-cameron/)**

By: [Dr\. Max Cameron](https://politics.ubc.ca/profile/maxwell-cameron/), Professor, Department of Political Science and School of Public Policy and Global Affairs

**What is your book about?**

This book analyzes the forces driving disunity in Canada and offers Canadians a path forward in rebuilding civic responsibility and finding common ground\.

**Why did you write this book?**

To contribute to the strength and unity of the Canadian civic community in response to the threats to our sovereignty from the United States under Donald Trump\.

View media coverage

*launch*

[Source link](https://www.cbc.ca/books/50-plus-canadian-nonfiction-titles-we-re-excited-about-this-spring-9.7080608)

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Richard-K.png)

### **[Mediatic Shakespeare: The Dynamics Of Orality, Script And Print In The Plays And Poems](https://utppublishing.com/doi/10.3138/9781487565367.001)**

By: [Dr\. Richard Cavell](https://english.ubc.ca/profile/richard-cavell/), Professor, Department of English Language and Literatures

**What is your book about?**

My book is about the media shift out of an oral culture into a print culture that was taking place during Shakespeare’s lifetime, and how that shift is dramatised in a number of his works\.

**Why did you write this book?**

Marshall McLuhan once said to me that he derived his media theory from Shakespeare\. This was my inspiration to write the book\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Barbara-D.png)

### **[The Language of Memes: Patterns of Meaning Emergence Across Image and Text](https://www.cambridge.org/ca/universitypress/subjects/languages-linguistics/cognitive-linguistics/language-memes-patterns-meaning-across-image-and-text?format=HB&isbn=9781108844352)**

By: [Dr\. Barbara Dancygier](http://faculty.arts.ubc.ca/bdancygier), Professor, Department of English Language and Literatures

**What is this book about?**

The book proposes a cognitive linguistic analysis of internet memes\. We show how image\-plus\-text contemporary artifacts instantiate and develop patterns of meaning emergence we have been seeing in language\. As we show, memes not only rely on pre\-existing linguistic conventions, but also establish new conventions which are well\-adjusted to the needs of online communication\. Far from being simplistic coinages of image and text, they create new standards of internet discourse\.

**Why did you write this book?**

For a while now, we have been puzzled by the fact that memes use deceptively simple forms to express a variety of interesting and relevant meanings\. They are very good at expressing opinions online without lengthy explanations\. We also found that memes stand out among other multimodal artifacts \(advertisements, campaign materials, posters, etc\.\) in that they use linguistic forms in specific and well\-structured ways\. We intended to draw attention to online discourse and its rules by discussing the ways in which language adjusts to the dominance of visual forms of expression\.

### **[Austrian German: a 300\-year love story \[Österreichisches Deutsch: eine 300\-jährige Liebesgeschichte\]](https://www.newacademicpress.at/gesamtverzeichnis/unkategorisiert/oesterreichisches-deutsch/)**

By: [Dr\. Stefan Dollinger](https://english.ubc.ca/profile/stefan-dollinger/), Professor, Department of English Language and Literatures, Canadian Word Centre

**What is your book about?**

This book reflects on Standard Austrian German, the dominant standard variety in Austria, examining its 500\-year history alongside 300 years of neglect, suppression, and misunderstanding within German philology, dialectology, and linguistics\. It showcases, for readers aged 14 and up, the unexplored biases in linguistics—some of which remain entangled, to this day, with National\-Socialist stances that were carried over into the present without ever being critically examined\. It tells the story of the hegemonization, and at times weaponization, of “standard German” from Germany, and of the deliberate backgrounding of Standard Austrian and Standard Swiss German for sociopolitical reasons since the 1860s\. Large\-scale data shows that 94\.3% of its speakers \(n\=70,000\) see Standard Austrian German as the “more suitable” standard for Austria\.

**Why did you write this book?**

It’s a question of linguistic justice\. I noticed that what is done internationally in sociolinguistics is incompatible with the way German dialectologists and sociolinguists work on what they call “German in Austria\.” The name — it used to be “Austrian German” — is itself their program\. I had to speak up\. I started in 2016 with a methodological paper, then followed up in 2019 with a book\. The response was so negative and ad hominem that I decided to dig through the archives instead\. What I found was a story worse than I could have imagined: linguists who had acted as Nazi desk perpetrators, then went on to be celebrated after 1945\. What counts as “the German language” is an important question, and the answer looks very different in the 2020s — yet the field, by and large, still relies on a definition from the 1820s, straight out of the Grimms’ storybook\.

This collection, co\-edited with Sarah Crover, considers how queens in Renaissance England were complicit in, confronted, complicated, or were sidelined by England’s growing nationalist energies\. Tudor, Stuart, French, Scottish, historical, present, and imaginary queens, consorts, princesses and regents all participated in the fractured politics of England\-as\-concept\. **What is your book about?**

*The Long Rise of the British Novel, 1660\-1800* presents a new thesis on the rise and development of the modern novel over the entirety of the eighteenth century\. It challenges the widely received notion that the rise of capitalism fostered the individualism of realist fiction in the Victorian age characteristic of the novel\. I argue instead that the novel evolved as a form typically opposed to capitalist greed and celebrating empathetic social interaction\. My book also argues that women writers, particularly Frances Burney and Charlotte Smith, created the first realist fiction in the late eighteenth century\. Though largely forgotten in the nineteenth century, these authors shaped the form of realist fiction from the Victorian age to the present day\.

**Why did you write this book?**

I believed that reigning theories on the origins of the novel were mistaken in important respects\.

**What is your book about?**

I had the pleasure of collaborating with Chisasibi Eeyou poet Margaret Sam\-Cromarty to put together this volume of her life works\. Born in 1936 on Fort George Island, Margaret began writing in her 50s, after her family was relocated to Chisasibi for the La Grande hydroelectric project\. This event informs much of her poetry, which explores family, community life, and her experiences of the land both before and after the move\. Thirty years after publishing her first book in 1992, Margaret revisited her poetry and stories to bring them into the hands of a new generation of readers\. This book is a testament to her role in keeping Eeyou knowledge alive and is essential reading to understand a Cree woman’s life story and her perspective on political power in James Bay in the late 20th century\.

**Why did you write this book?**

Margaret Sam\-Cromarty is the “Poet Laureate of Eeyou Istchee” but is little\-known outside of James Bay\. Though out of print for years, her books remained in high demand within her community\. As an Anglophone First Nations author in Quebec, writing at a time when the province’s literary scene gave little attention to Indigenous voices, her work fell into an in\-between and has, until now, been absent from scholarly work on this corpus\. We worked with the “First Voices First Texts” series at UMP, which is committed to reconnecting contemporary readers with unjustly neglected classics of Indigenous literature\. Without any doubt, Margaret’s poetry and stories make a significant contribution to the field of Indigenous literatures in Quebec and Canada\.

Organized through four lenses, the book revisits established classics and controversial works; highlights films and filmmaking from often\-overlooked regions and cultures; explores “weird” films and unconventional performances; and foregrounds underrepresented voices, including diaspora cinema, political films, and works addressing addiction, dispossession, and cross\-border communities\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Gaoheng-Z2.png)

### **[Fashion Communications between Italy and China: Unfolding a Sartorial Relationship](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/fashion-communications-between-italy-and-china-9781350544062/)**

By: [Dr\. Gaoheng Zhang](https://fhis.ubc.ca/profile/gaoheng-zhang/), Associate Professor, Department of French, Hispanic, and Italian Studies

 **What is your book about?**

In this in\-depth study, I analyzed the relationship between the Italian ready\-to\-wear fashion industry and the Chinese fast fashion industry, focussing on the 2000s and 2010s\.

> 
> Congratulations to the six UBC Arts researchers who received funding through the 2026 Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada \(NSERC\) Discovery Grants and Discovery Launch Supplement program\.

This grant supports long\-term research programs, recognizing the creativity and innovation that drive discovery forward\. Learn more about the recipients and their projects below\.

---

### **Discovery Grant recipients**

The [NSERC Discovery Grants](https://www.nserc-crsng.gc.ca/professors-professeurs/grants-subs/dgigp-psigp_eng.asp) program supports ongoing programs of research with long\-term goals rather than a single short\-term project or collection of projects\. 

-   **[Dr\. Muhammad Abdul\-Mageed](https://linguistics.ubc.ca/profile/muhammad-abdul-mageed/)**, Department of Linguistics  
    Project: Efficient and methodic reasoning for transformative low\-resource natural language processing  
    
-   [**Dr\. Bryan Gick**](https://linguistics.ubc.ca/profile/bryan-gick/), Department of Linguistics  
    Project: Characterizing posture across communicative fine motor systems
-   [**Dr\. Darko Odic**](https://psych.ubc.ca/profile/darko-odic/), Department of Psychology  
    Project: Investigating the mechanisms and development of internal number perception
-   [**Dr\. Daniela Palombo**](https://psych.ubc.ca/profile/daniela-palombo/), Department of Psychology  
    Project: Emotional spillover: Exploring the retroactive effects of emotion on memory for predictive information
-   **[Dr\. Camilla Speller](https://anth.ubc.ca/profile/camilla-speller/),** Department of Anthropology  
    Project: Documenting millennia of marine biodiversity and Indigenous stewardship through biomolecular archives

---

### **Discovery Launch Supplement recipient**

Discovery Launch Supplements provide timely resources to support early career researchers as they establish a Discovery Grant\-funded research program\. The following project was awarded an additional Discovery Launch Supplement of $12,500\. 

-   **[Dr\. Tianjia Liu](https://geog.ubc.ca/profile/tianjia-liu/),** Department of Geography  
    Project: Mapping and modeling wildfires and smoke under land management interventions and climate extremes
