title: UBC launches the first free open-access Nepali textbook
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Nepali-textbook1.png)

The UBC Nepali Language team at the launch of the *Introduction to the Nepali Language* textbook at Nepal Heritage Day BC on May 30, 2026\. From left to right: Binod Shrestha, Dr\. Mark Turin, and Salina Dolmo Lama\.

> *Introduction to the Nepali Language* is the first free open\-access textbook of its kind designed for learners, educators, community groups, and heritage speakers of Nepali\.  The book was launched in celebration of BC’s first\-ever Nepali Heritage Day on 30 May, 2026, marking an important milestone in expanding opportunities for Nepali language learning and engagement\.

Developed within the Faculty of Arts, the textbook was created through a collaboration between faculty, students, and staff\. The team included principal investigator [Dr\. Mark Turin](https://markturin.arts.ubc.ca/), an Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology and the Institute for Critical Indigenous Studies; [Binod Shrestha](https://himalaya.arts.ubc.ca/language-instructors/), an instructor with the Himalaya Program; and [Salina Dolmo Lama](https://www.linkedin.com/in/salina-dolmo-lama/), a Nepali graduate student at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs\.

The project also received support from the Open Education Resources \(OER\) Affordability Grant Program and was enhanced by contributions from the UBC Library’s Scholarly Communications team and open education infrastructure supported by the Centre for Teaching, Learning and Technology \(CTLT\)\.

We spoke with Dr\. Turin and Salina Lama about the journey behind the textbook and what this new resource means for learners in the Himalayan region and the global Nepali diaspora\. [Erin Fields](https://directory.library.ubc.ca/people/view/798), [Open Education and Scholarly Communication Librarian](https://scholcomm.ubc.ca/open-scholarship/open-education/) at the UBC Library, also shared a behind\-the\-scenes look at the collaborative effort and careful work that made the project possible\.

---

### **What led you to develop this open access textbook? Was there a gap or need you were hoping to address?**

**Dr\. Turin:** I have lived and worked in Nepal since the early 1990s, and over the years I have learned, taught, and translated Nepali in a range of professional capacities\. I love speaking and teaching Nepali and have long wanted to build a tool like this\.

The textbook grew out of a collaboration with Binod Shrestha, whose applied Nepali teaching in Nepal and North America spans decades, and Salina Dolmo Lama, whose cultural knowledge and community\-informed perspective shaped the resource throughout\.

Over the past decade, through the UBC Himalaya Program and Binod Shrestha’s intensive summer Nepali teaching, we have become increasingly aware of a real absence\. Nepali language is central to Nepal, to Himalayan studies, and to a fast\-growing global diaspora across the Gulf, East and Southeast Asia, Europe, North America, and Australia\. Yet rigorous, accessible, open introductory materials for university and community learners remain surprisingly scarce\.

We wanted to create a structured, multimedia resource that meets those learners where they are: one that begins with Devanāgarī — the script used to write Nepali and several other South Asian languages — and pronunciation, and then builds speaking, listening, reading, writing, grammar, and cultural understanding together, in a single, freely accessible place\.

Today’s learners are diverse\. They include heritage speakers and diaspora families, community schools and weekend classes, independent and online learners\. Many are second\-generation Nepalis who understand the language but do not speak it confidently, or who speak it but cannot read Devanāgarī\. For them, Nepali is not a foreign language at all, but one of ancestry, family, and belonging — something to reclaim rather than acquire from the outside\. My essay [“Who Learns Nepali Now?”](https://commons-nepal.com/who-learns-nepali-now/) in The Commons might give a more comprehensive idea on this\.

---

### **How does this project fit into your other work, especially in connection with communities in the Himalayan region and the Pacific Northwest?**

**Dr\. Turin:** It gives us a model\. The project shows that community\-engaged language work can be serious scholarship, a form of public humanities, and public pedagogy at once\. And it strengthens UBC’s role as a bridge between campus\-based teaching and the wider Himalayan and Nepali communities of British Columbia, the Pacific Northwest, and beyond\.

It also gives us practical experience — with open platforms, accessibility standards, audio\-supported learning, and the practice of responsive and iterative revision — that can inform future work with Tibetan and other Himalayan languages, and that resonates with the collaborative, community\-led language projects we are involved in with Indigenous partners here in this region\.

Perhaps most importantly, it helps make language work visible\. Languages do not sustain themselves on goodwill alone — they need materials, platforms, teachers, and institutions willing to invest for the long term\.

---

“The project contributes to the visibility of Nepali, but also to a larger conversation — about linguistic justice, cultural knowledge, and the kinds of digital resources that underrepresented languages increasingly depend on\.”

Dr\. Mark Turin

Associate Professor, Department of Anthropology and Institute for Critical Indigenous Studies

---

### **Why was it important that this resource be freely available, and what do you hope learners take away beyond language skills?**

**Dr\. Turin:** A free, open resource can move around and be shared more easily — through community schools, family networks, university classes, study groups, and diaspora organisations\. And because it is open, it is not finished in the way a printed textbook is\. Language learning is never really complete; it is recursive, social, and situated\. So we have built something that can be revised, corrected, and expanded as learners and teachers tell us what actually works\. A living resource like this reflects how language is genuinely learned far better than a closed one\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/IMG_5362-scaled.jpg)

Binod Shrestha and Salina Dolmo Lama audio recording at UBC Studios on February 20, 2026\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/626A4552-scaled.jpg)

Binod Shrestha presenting the resource at the Nepali Heritage Day BC event\.

[Image](https://artf.cms.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/image-1-scaled.jpeg)

UBC Himalaya team with Premier David Eby, MLA for Surrey\-Fleetwood Jagrup Brar, and President of Nepal Cultural Society of BC, Raju Bhattarai\.

### **What was your role and how did you contribute to the creation of this textbook?**

**Salina D\. Lama:** In the first phase of the project, I supported the development and review of the resource content, contributed cultural and linguistic perspectives, and helped ensure the material was accurate, accessible, and relevant for today’s learners\. I also recorded the female voice for the dialogue\-based learning content\.

Now that the resource is published and was launched at BC’s first Nepali Heritage Day, my role has shifted to outreach — raising awareness among community organizations, educators, and academic repositories, and gathering feedback from learners so the resource keeps improving over time\.

---

### **Did anything about this project surprise you? Was there anything that was particularly challenging?**

**Salina D\. Lama:** One of the most surprising parts of this project was working with Pressbooks and realizing how much flexibility it offers for creating learning materials\. I did not expect the platform to be so dynamic in terms of design, structure, and how content can be presented, especially while working with Devanāgarī script\. That made me think differently about how digital tools can support education, especially at a  time when language learning is being shaped by  emerging technology and interactive platforms\. It also made the process feel more creative than I initially expected, because there was room to think about how learners would experience the material, not just what content needed to be included\.

One of the main challenges was thinking carefully about accessibility for learners of different abilities and at different levels\. Language learning is never a single\-track process, and it became important to make sure that the material could support all kinds of learners in a meaningful way\.

---

“I learned about the value of designing policies and programs that reflect the needs and experiences of the communities they serve\. Working on this project allows me to apply these ideas in practice where community feedback and input will shape the living resource\.”

Salina Dolmo Lama

Master's student \(MPPGA\), IAR Fellow with the Himalaya Program

---

### **How does this experience fit into your broader career aspirations, or your research work?**

**Salina D\. Lama:** This project has encouraged me to think more deeply about knowledge equity and who gets to participate in education and digital knowledge systems\. One aspect that stood out for me was working in a team where none of us had Nepali as our only or first language, but where all of us still had strong connections to it in different ways\. That mix shaped a collaborative process drawing on different experiences and approaches to the language\. More importantly, bringing those different relationships to  language into the same space helped us create something thoughtful and accountable\.

At the same time, my own background in a multilingual environment, including speaking Tamang as my mother tongue alongside Nepali, has shaped how I understand language as something closely tied to identity, visibility, and belonging\. In Nepal and in diaspora contexts, language often carries different levels of recognition and presence in formal education and public spaces\. This has made me more curious about how language shapes  those experiences, particularly for Indigenous and minority communities from Nepal who speak their own mother tongues alongside Nepali as the national language, and in diasporic settings where they navigate English as a dominant language—sometimes as a first language for second\- or third\-generation families\.

---

### **What role did the UBC Library play in bringing this open\-access Nepali language textbook to publication?**

**Erin Fields:** We assisted with developing the style and structure of the book—including developing a style guide and creating custom coding—to make sure it was standardized and visually\-flowed for the users\. We also provided guidance on copyright and licensing, developed metadata, and created a discovery and dissemination plan to make the textbook widely accessible through open education networks, repositories, and language\-learning communities\.

Before publication, we conducted a technical review and final clean\-up, transitioned the book to its permanent URL, and registered its DOI through Datacite\. Throughout the project, we provided training, answered questions as they arose, and met regularly with the project team to ensure we were working toward shared goals\.

---

“Open educational resource development takes a deep commitment to the open, equitable, and free sharing of knowledge that not only supports learning for all but also, in the instance of the *Introduction to Nepali*, builds cultural bridges through the learning of language\. We are proud to have been a part of this publication\.”

Erin Fields

Open Education and Scholarly Communications Librarian, Digital Programs & Services

---

Download the book

Introduction to the Nepali Language is a free, open\-access textbook for learners, educators, community organizations, and heritage speakers interested in studying Nepali\.

**Get access**

[Source link](https://pressbooks.bccampus.ca/nepali/)

---

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/07/Sohana.png) *Sohana Manzoor is a Communications and Storytelling Assistant with the Faculty of Arts Communications team\. She is currently completing her Master of Fine Arts in Creative Writing at UBC\.*

title: Speaking Arts: A glossary
content_markdown:
> Stepping into university comes with a whole new vocabulary\. Some of it is specific to Canadian universities, some is unique to UBC, and some is specific to the Faculty of Arts\.
> 
> Here’s a plain\-language guide to the terms you’ll see most often\.

---

## A\-D

### A

**[Academic Accommodations](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/academic-learning-resources/academic-accommodations-disabilities/)**: Support that reduces barriers in the learning environment for students with disabilities or ongoing medical conditions\. The [Centre for Accessibility](https://students.ubc.ca/about-student-services/centre-for-accessibility/) determines eligibility and the accommodations available based on a student’s individual needs\.

**[Academic Calendar](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/)**: The Calendar is a comprehensive guide to all programs, courses, services, and policies at the University of British Columbia\. The Calendar serves as a record of many University academic policies and procedures\.

**[Academic Concession](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-arts/academic-concession)**: Support, like a deadline extension or deferred exam, for students facing unanticipated events that interfere with their academic work, applied with fairness, flexibility, and compassion under [UBC’s Academic Concession policy](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/academic-concession)\. \([Visit Arts Advising](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/student-support/academic-support/academic-advising/)\)

**[Academic Progress Report \(APR\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/year-by-year-planning/academic-progress-report/)**: An essential tool in Workday that helps you keep track of your degree requirements and credits\.

**[Add/Drop Period](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/dates-deadlines/)**: The first weeks of term when you can still adjust your course schedule without academic or financial penalty\.

**[AMS \(Alma Mater Society\)](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/)**: UBC’s undergraduate student union — runs clubs, services, health and dental plans, and events across campus\.

**[Arts Academic Advising](https://arts.ubc.ca/student-support/academic-support/academic-advising/)**: Advisors specific to the Faculty of Arts who help with course selection, major declaration, and degree requirements once you’re in the Faculty\.

**[Arts Indigenous Student Advising \(AISA\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/student-support/academic-support/arts-indigenous-student-advising/)**: Arts Indigenous Student Advising in the Faculty of Arts supports the success of First Nations, Métis, and Inuit students\.

**[Arts Credit Minimum Requirement](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-arts/credit-requirements-and-regulations)**: The minimum number of credits you must complete within Faculty of Arts courses specifically, ensuring your degree stays grounded in Arts even if you take courses in other Faculties\.

**[Arts One](https://artsone.arts.ubc.ca/)**: A first\-year program where one small group of students takes an interdisciplinary, discussion\-based course together across a full year\.

**[AUS \(Arts Undergraduate Society\)](https://www.ubcaus.ca/)**: The student society specifically for Arts undergrads, separate from the campus\-wide AMS\. The AUS runs Arts\-specific clubs, events, and represents Arts students’ interests within the Faculty\.

**[Award](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/student-support/funding/)**: Funding you can apply for that may recognize things like your lived experience, leadership, volunteering, community involvement, or academic achievements, not just your grades\. Most awards include a monetary prize\. The term “award” is sometimes used as a catch\-all term for awards, scholarships, prizes, and bursaries\. \([See scholarship, prize, and bursary](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/guide-to-arts-scholarships-and-awards/)\)

---

### B

**[Bachelor of Arts \(BA\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/)**: The most common degree in the Faculty of Arts, and flexible by design\. You’ll explore multiple subjects before committing to a specialization\.

Beyond the BA, The Faculty of Arts also offers several specialized degrees for students with a focused interest from day one, including:

**[Bachelor of Fine Arts \(BFA\)](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-fine-arts/introduction)**: A four\-year degree blending artistic and professional practice, theory, and research\. Offered in Creative Writing, Film Production, Theatre \(Acting\), Theatre \(Design and Production\), and Visual Art\.

**[Bachelor of International Economics \(BIE\)](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/vancouver-school-economics/bachelor-international-economics)**: A four\-year degree offered jointly by the Vancouver School of Economics and the Sauder School of Business, with intensive study in international trade, finance, and development\.

**[Bachelor of Media Studies \(BMS\)](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-media-studies)**: A four\-year, interdisciplinary cohort program blending practice, theory, and research, with courses drawn from eight participating units across Arts — from Computer Science and English to Journalism, Writing, and Media\.

**[Bachelor of Music \(BMus\)](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/school-music/bachelor-music)**: A four\-year degree with a core curriculum in music theory, aural skills, history, technology, and solo and ensemble performance, alongside liberal arts electives\. Standards align with the Canadian University Music Society\.

**[Bachelor of Social Work \(BSW\)](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/school-social-work/bachelor-social-work)**: Completed in two years full\-time or three years part\-time, covering theory, policy, research, and practice\. A Canadian Association for Social Work Education \(CASWE\) accredited degree preparing you for generalist social work practice, grounded in critical thinking and issues of power, discrimination, and social justice\.

**[Bachelor \+ Master of Management \(B\+MM\)](https://www.sauder.ubc.ca/programs/dual-degrees/bachelor-and-master-management)**: A unique dual degree program that combines your undergraduate studies with a world\-class business education\.

**Bursary**: A non\-repayable, need\-based award\. This fills the gap between your student loans and what you still need, if you’re a domestic student\. \([See scholarship, prize, and award](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/guide-to-arts-scholarships-and-awards/)\)

---

### C

**[Campus\-Wide Login \(CWL\)](https://www.myaccount.ubc.ca/myAccount/)**: This allows you to register for courses, check your UBC accounts \(E\.g\., Canvas, Workday\), and log on to UBC wireless internet and UBC systems\.

**[Canvas](https://about.canvas.ubc.ca/)**: The learning platform instructors use to post syllabi, readings, assignments, and grades for each course\.

**[Centre for Accessibility \(CFA\)](https://students.ubc.ca/about-student-services/centre-for-accessibility/)**: UBC’s office supporting students with disabilities or ongoing health conditions, helping arrange academic accommodations like extra time, note\-taking support, or alternative assignment formats\.

**[Co\-op, Arts](https://artscoop.ubc.ca/)**: An optional program combining paid work terms with your degree, letting you graduate with professional experience alongside your BA\.

**[Continuing Studies](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/programs/arts-professional-continuing-education/)**: UBC offers non\-credit courses and certificate programs, including preparatory writing and math courses and the English Language Institute\.

**[Coordinated Arts Program \(CAP\)](https://cap.arts.ubc.ca/)**: A first\-year option where you take a themed cluster of courses alongside the same group of classmates\. It’s a nice way to build community while meeting core requirements\.

**[Corequisite](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/introduction#:~:text=for%20more%20information.-,Prerequisites%20and%20Corequisites,-If%20specific%20studies)**: A corequisite is a course that you must take prior to, or concurrently with, a selected course\. It is important to investigate which prerequisites and corequisites may be required for courses you want to take later\.

**[Course Numbering](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions)**: Course names have multiple components\. A course code like LING\_V 101 R01 breaks down into subject \(LING \= Linguistics\), campus \(\_V \= Vancouver\), course level \(101\), and section \(R01, indicating a specific time slot or term\)\. [Check out the full list of courses](https://courses.students.ubc.ca/course-search)\.

**[Course Planning](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/tips-for-first-year-course-planning/)**: The process of choosing your courses each term based on your program requirements, prerequisites, and interests — something you are encouraged to start in your first year, working closely with Arts Academic Advising\.

**[Credits](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-arts/credit-requirements-and-regulations)**: The unit used to measure course workload and progress toward your degree\. Most Arts courses are worth 3 credits, which is equivalent to one class\. For example, 15 credits are equal to 5 courses\.

---

### D

**[Degree requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)**: The set of courses and credit minimums every Arts student must complete beyond their major or program — including breadth, upper\-level, and Faculty\-wide requirements — to graduate\.

**[Degree Planning](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/)**: Plan your undergraduate degree with useful resources to help guide you along your academic journey — from entering your first year as an Arts student to receiving your degree\.

**Double Counting**: Using a single upper\-level course to satisfy requirements in two different programs at once \(like a double major\)\. Credit limits apply, and you still only earn credit for the course once, even if it counts toward two sets of requirements\.

**[Double Major](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-arts/degree-program-options)**: Combines two majors within a single degree, allowing you to meet the requirements of both without extending your program length\.

**[Dual Degree](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/programs/degree-options/)**: Combines two separate degrees into one combined program, typically taking longer than a single degree but resulting in two credentials\.

---

## E\-H

### E

**[Elective](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/understanding-electives/)**: Beyond your program and [degree requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/), the rest are electives — courses outside your specialization that let you explore other interests\. Single\-major students take roughly half their credits as electives; double majors or minors take fewer\.

**[Enrolment Services Advisors \(ESA\)](https://students.ubc.ca/about-student-services/enrolment-services-advisors/)**: Staff who can help with registration, transcripts, and general degree\-planning questions before you’ve connected with an Arts advisor\.

**[Exams](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/exams)**: Formal examination period at UBC\. The Winter Session exams are held in December and April\. Enrolment Services schedules your exams, and shares the schedule toward the end of each Term\.

**[Exchange](https://goglobal.ubc.ca/go-global/programs-ubc-students/exchange)**: A Go Global option letting you study for a term or year at one of UBC’s partner universities abroad, paying UBC tuition while earning credits that transfer back to your degree\.

---

### F

**Faculty**: There are two definitions of faculty at UBC:

-   1\. A division or unit of the university dedicated to a specific area of study, often split into departments and schools\.
-   2\. The deans, professors, lecturers, and researchers who make up the units\.

---

### G

**[Go Global](https://goglobal.ubc.ca/)**: UBC’s hub for international learning opportunities, including exchange programs, study abroad, group study, and research or work placements abroad\.

**[GPA](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/academic-performance/promotion-continuation-grading/)**: Your Grade Point Average, calculated on a scale out of 4\.33 at UBC, used for academic standing, scholarships, and program requirements like Honours\.

**[Grades](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/courses/grades)**: For grading, UBC uses a percentage scale and equivalent letter grades\. Your grades contribute to your GPA\.

**[Graduate student](https://www.ubc.ca/graduate-students/)**: A student who is completing a master’s or doctoral degree\.

---

### H

**[Honours](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-arts/bachelor-arts/degree-program-options)**: A more intensive version of a major, usually with a higher GPA requirement and often a research or thesis component\. It’s not a requirement, but an option if you want to go deeper into a subject\.

**[Housing](https://vancouver.housing.ubc.ca/)**: On\-campus housing options ranging from eight\-month residences for first\-year students to year\-round residences for upper\-year and graduate students, plus family accommodation\.

---

## I\-N

### I

**[Imagine UBC](https://students.ubc.ca/campus-life/involved/ubc-orientation-transition-leadership/imagine-ubc-orientation-leaders/)**: A campus\-wide welcome day at the start of the Winter Session in September, with Faculty\-specific events to introduce new students to Arts\.

**[Interdisciplinary](https://interdisciplinary.arts.ubc.ca/)**: Combines ideas and methods from different subjects \(disciplines\) to understand, study, or solve a problem\. eg\. using ideas from geography and art together to study how patterns form in nature\.

**[International Student Advising](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/international-student-advising/)**: Get help with your study permit, health insurance, and adjusting to life in Canada\. Advisors are certified and trained specifically to support you\.

---

### J

**[Jump Start](https://you.ubc.ca/jump-start-vancouver/)**: UBC’s early\-arrival orientation program, especially popular with international and out\-of\-province students, offers a head start on campus life before Winter Session begins\.

---

### M

**[Major](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/year-by-year-planning/add-major-minor/)**: Your primary area of study within the BA, declared partway through your degree \(not on day one\)\. Most Arts students choose their major at the end of first year\.

**[Minor](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/year-by-year-planning/add-major-minor/)**: A secondary area of focus that requires less credits than a major\. Getting a minor adds depth in a second subject alongside your major\.

**[Musqueam](https://indigenous.ubc.ca/indigenous-engagement/musqueam-and-ubc/)**: UBC Vancouver is located on the traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Musqueam people\. The land it is situated on has always been a place of learning for the Musqueam, who for millennia have passed on their culture, history, and traditions from one generation to the next on this site\.

---

### N

**[The Nest](https://visit.ubc.ca/eat-drink-and-stay/restaurants/food-courts/ams-nest-food-court/)**: The student union building, home to AMS services, event space, and a food hall with campus favourites like Blue Chip and The Delly, among many others\.

---

## O\-S

### O

**Office Hours**: Set times each week when instructors and TAs are available for drop\-in questions, one of the most underused resources by new students\.

**[Orientation Leader \(OL\)](https://students.ubc.ca/campus-life/involved/ubc-orientation-transition-leadership/)**: A current student volunteer who runs welcome activities during Jump Start and Imagine Day\. They’re often one of the first friendly, upper\-year faces that you meet on campus\.

**[Outside requirement](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/)**: You must complete a minimum number of credits outside your field of study, often fulfilled through electives\. Single majors require 60 outside credits; adding a minor, honours, combined major, double major, or double honours reduces that number\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

---

### P

**[Place and Power](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/get-in-the-know-about-ways-of-knowing/)**: A 3\-credit requirement exploring the history and current realities of the xwməθkwəy̓əm \(Musqueam\) and the land UBC sits on, alongside Vancouver and BC’s broader systems of power and inequality\. It can be fulfilled through an approved course in any discipline, including your own program, at any point in your degree\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

**[Prerequisite](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/course-descriptions/introduction#:~:text=for%20more%20information.-,Prerequisites%20and%20Corequisites,-If%20specific%20studies)**: Prerequisites are specific courses that you must complete before you can take upper\-level courses\. Course descriptions show prerequisites where applicable\.

**Prize**: Given if you’re the top student in a specific class\. Usually, no application is required\. \([See scholarship, award, and bursary](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/guide-to-arts-scholarships-and-awards/)\)

**[Professional programs](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-commerce-and-business-administration/professional-and-diploma-courses)**: A program entered after full or partial completion of a Bachelor’s degree, training you for a specialized professional field like Medicine, Dentistry, Law, or Social Work\.

**[Programs](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/programs/program-options/)**: The series of courses that leads to a particular degree\.

**[Prospective student](https://www.ubc.ca/prospective-students/)**: A student who is thinking about applying to UBC\.

---

### R

**[Reading Week](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/dates-and-deadlines)**: A scheduled period during Winter Term 2 when regular classes and lectures are cancelled to give you time to rest, catch up on coursework, and study for midterms\. \([See WT1 Midterm Break](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/dates-and-deadlines)\)

**[Registration](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/registration)**: The period where you select the courses you will take in your next year\. Registration for Winter Session runs from mid\-late June \(first\- and fourth\-years\) and early\-mid July \(second\- and third\-years\)\.

**[Registration appointment](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/registration/registration-dates/)**: Before you register for courses, you will receive an email from Enrolment Services with an assigned date and time when you will be able to start registering in courses\.

**[Research Requirement](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/)**: A 3\-credit course, typically specific to your major, where you contribute to scholarship in your field — completed between 30 and 120 credits into your degree\. These courses often carry prerequisites, so it’s worth planning ahead\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

---

### S

**Scholarship**: Based purely on your academic achievements\. The good news is some of these are automatic and tied straight to your grades\. \([See award, prize, and bursary](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/guide-to-arts-scholarships-and-awards/)\)

**[Session](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/dates-and-deadlines)**: At UBC, a Session refers to the Winter or Summer period when classes are offered, and each Winter s\\Session is composed of two terms\.

**[Six\-Week StART](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/six-week-start/)**: A free transition program that connects every new\-to\-UBC Arts student with an upper\-year Orientation Leader\.

**Standard Program**: The UBC Calendar’s term for building your timetable by choosing courses each term\.

**[Standard Timetable](https://courses.students.ubc.ca/standard-timetables)**: UBC Registration’s term for programs with a pre\-planned timetable of linked courses that must be taken as a whole \(E\.g\., [CAP](https://cap.arts.ubc.ca/), [ArtsOne](https://artsone.arts.ubc.ca/)\)

**[Summer Session](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/dates-and-deadlines)**: Two optional terms running May to August\. Take summer courses to lighten a future term’s course load, or catch up on your requirements\.

**[Syllabus](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/content-and-distribution-course-syllabi)**: The course outline, given at the start of term, laying out readings, assignments, deadlines, and grading\. Professors expect students to read the syllabus at the beginning of the term, and continue to refer to it throughout the course\. Check your syllabus first when you have questions about deadlines or policies\.

---

## T\-W

### T

**[Teaching Assistant \(TA\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/about/academic-postings/)**: A graduate \(or sometimes senior undergraduate\) student who supports a course — running discussion sections, marking, and holding office hours\.

**Term**: What UBC calls a semester \(or “quarter” at some schools\)\. A term is one of two study periods making up the Winter Session, each about four months long\.

**[Thunderbirds](https://brand.ubc.ca/guidelines/thunderbirds/)**: UBC’s varsity athletics program, competing since 1915 and holding more intercollegiate championships than any other Canadian university \(alumni include 241 Olympians\)

**[Transcript](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/campus-wide-policies-and-regulations/transcript-academic-record)**: A document listing grades for all courses in all semesters at a particular school or university\.

**Transfer student**: A student who has completed some post\-secondary studies elsewhere, either at another university or college, or in a different Faculty at UBC, and has moved to Arts to continue their degree or diploma\.

**[Tuum Est](https://brand.ubc.ca/about-ubc-brand/)**: The UBC motto\. Latin for “It is yours\.”

---

### U

**[U\-Pass BC](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/u-pass/)**: A subsidized transit pass giving you access to public transit across Metro Vancouver, costing $187\.60 per term for a full 3\-Zone Pass each month\.

**[UBCcard](https://ubccard.ubc.ca/)**: Your official student ID — used for building access, library services, and often U\-Pass transit\.

**[Undergraduate student](https://www.ubc.ca/undergraduate-students/)**: Any student in a Bachelor’s degree program\.

**[Upper\-level requirement](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/)**: You must complete a minimum number of upper\-level credits \(numbered 300\+\)\. Single majors, combined majors, and Interdisciplinary Studies \(IDST\) require 48 credits; honours, double major, major/honours, or double honours programs require more\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

---

### V

**[Visiting students](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/faculties-colleges-and-schools/faculty-graduate-and-postdoctoral-studies/admission/visiting-students)**: A student enrolled at another university who is taking courses at UBC for credit at their home university\.

---

### W

**[Waitlist](https://you.ubc.ca/applying-ubc/applied/)**: A queue for a full course\. A spot on the waitlist doesn’t guarantee a seat, so it’s worth having a backup course in mind\.

**[Ways of Knowing Breadth Requirement](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)**: An interdisciplinary foundation of the BA degree requirements that will empower you to explore different ways of building knowledge across four different areas of study\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

**[Withdrawal \(“W”\)](https://students.ubc.ca/enrolment/dates-deadlines/)**: Dropping a course after the add/drop deadline up until the final withdrawal deadline each term\. You won’t receive a grade, but a “W” appears on your transcript\.

**[Winter Session](https://vancouver.calendar.ubc.ca/dates-and-deadlines)**: The main academic year, running September to April and split into two terms \(Term 1 and Term 2\)\.

**[Writing Requirement](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/bachelor-of-arts/)**: 3\-credit course building university\-level writing skills, meant to be completed in your first year or first 30 credits\. Miss the 54\-credit deadline \(or your first year, for transfer students\), and your registration will be blocked until Arts Academic Advising approves a plan to complete the requirement\. \([See Degree Requirements](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/degree-planning/degree-requirements/)\)

**[Work Learn](https://students.ubc.ca/career/work-learn-program/)**: A need\-based aid program letting qualified students work up to 10 hours a week on campus, often in roles related to their field of study\.

**[Workday](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/student-support/asc-student/)**: UBC’s system for registering in courses, checking your academic record, paying tuition, and managing your student account\.

title: UBC Arts researchers awarded SSHRC funding to advance social, cultural, and economic research
content_markdown:
> [Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2024/02/Web_award_pattern2.jpg)
> 
> UBC Faculty of Arts researchers are advancing 58 projects supported through the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council \(SSHRC\)’s Insight, Insight Development, and Partnership Development Grant competitions\.

The funded projects span a wide range of research areas, including artificial intelligence and digital literacies, climate change and sustainability, cultural histories, Indigenous\-led methodologies, labour inequalities, and social change\. Explore the Arts recipients and their research projects below\.

---

### **Insight Grants**

[Insight Grants](https://sshrc-crsh.canada.ca/en/funding/opportunities/insight-grants/2024/competition.aspx) support research excellence in the social sciences and humanities\. Funding is available to both emerging scholars and established scholars for research initiatives of two to five years\.

    Project led by Dr\. Lori Brotto, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology  
    Project: Shifting focus: Examining the impact of mindfulness on visual attention and sexual response in women and gender\-diverse individuals with and without sexual concerns

title: Arts in the Media: July 2026
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2020/01/About-Banner-Buchanan-Courtyard-UBC-Arts.jpg)

> This month, UBC Arts faculty were featured in media outlets including *CBC, BBC, Politico, The Washington Post*, and *Forbes*\. Their expertise informed stories ranging from the real\-world history behind *The Odyssey* and the global story of pepper to AI and online regulation, B\.C\. politics, and the science of happiness and well\-being\.

---

### **Centre for the Study of Democratic Institutions**

**How AI will fragment the internet  
**Dr\. Heidi Tworek said a single global standard for AI language models and freedom of expression is unlikely, noting that differing national approaches make universal regulation difficult to achieve\.  
[Politico](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/digital-future-daily/2026/07/20/how-ai-will-fragment-the-internet-01004989)

---

### **Department of Ancient, Mediterranean and Near Eastern Studies**

**‘The Odyssey’: Who were the real\-life people from the sea?  
**Dr\. Megan Daniels said the Sea Peoples were both a symptom and a cause of Bronze Age instability, noting that migration and raiding often emerged as responses to wider social and environmental disruptions\.  
[Mashable](https://mashable.com/entertainment/the-odyssey-sea-peoples-explainer)

---

### **Department of Asian Studies**

**A daily grind — The story of pepper  
**Dr\. Sebastian Prange discussed the history of pepper, exploring how its global trade shaped economies, cultures, and connections across the medieval world\.  
[ABC Radio](https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/every-bite/a-daily-grind-the-story-of-pepper/106882838)

---

### **Department of Geography**

**Analysis: 84% of nations miss deadline to identify ‘nature\-harming’ subsidies by 2025  
**Dr\. Jessica Dempsey said she would “absolutely” consider fossil\-fuel subsidies to be biodiversity\-harming, not only as a driver of climate change, but also because the extraction of fossil fuels can cause localised harms to biodiversity\.  
[Carbon Brief](https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-84-of-nations-miss-deadline-to-identify-nature-harming-subsidies-by-2025)

**10 essential reads to understand the impact of AI  
**Naomi Klein’s book *Doppelganger* is featured in the list\.[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/books/10-essential-reads-to-understand-the-impact-of-ai-9.7277027)

---

### **Department of History**

**How inevitable was the rise of the Chinese communist party?  
**Dr\. Timothy Cheek argues that the rise of the Chinese Communist Party was not inevitable, but shaped by historical circumstances, including political instability, warfare, and individual decisions that determined China’s path in the 20th century\.  
[History Today](https://www.historytoday.com/archive/head-head/how-inevitable-was-rise-chinese-communist-party)

---

### **Department of Political Science**

**Vancouver mayor asks premier for urgent action on foreign influence at City Hall  
**Dr\. Max Cameron said public hearings should prioritize residents and those directly affected by council decisions, but criticized the mayor’s decision to involve police, arguing the issue should be handled as a political matter rather than a criminal one\.  
[Vancouver Sun](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/vancouver-mayor-asks-premier-for-urgent-action-on-foreign-influence-at-city-hall)

**Former B\.C\. Liberal MLA says centrist party is the answer for voters tired of ‘extremes’  
**Dr\. Stewart Prest said some of B\.C\. Conservative leader Kerry\-Lynne Findlay’s caucus appointments could alienate voters and create space for a centrist alternative, though he noted the province’s first\-past\-the\-post system makes it difficult for smaller parties to gain traction\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/former-b-c-liberal-mla-says-centrist-party-is-the-answer-for-voters-tired-of-extremes-9.7275000)

**BC Conservatives hire an Alberta separatist and far\-right media figure  
**Dr\. Stewart Prest said the B\.C\. Conservatives’ recent hires signal a deliberate shift away from traditional provincial Conservative politics toward a style closer to U\.S\. MAGA Republicanism, reflecting a broader strategic direction under leader Kerry\-Lynne Findlay\.  
[The Tyee](https://thetyee.ca/News/2026/07/17/BC-Conservatives-Hire-Alberta-Separatist/)

**Vancouver mayor’s office inquired about public plaza, FOI reveals  
**Dr\. Max Cameron said the case raises questions about the relationship between elected officials and political staff, potential conflicts of interest, and whether decisions serve the public interest, noting that even the appearance of a conflict can damage public trust\.  
[CTV News](https://www.ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/vancouver-mayors-office-inquired-about-public-plaza-foi-reveals/)

**Is there room for an oil shipping terminal at Roberts Bank with a second container port planned?  
**Dr\. Kathryn Harrison said the lack of clear answers about the project highlights a rushed decision\-making process, noting that major projects would typically move forward only after key details have been resolved\.  
[The Province](https://theprovince.com/business/oil-shipping-terminal-roberts-bank-second-container-port-planned-is-there-room)

**Why bridge and tunnel politics helped make the B\.C\.\-Ottawa pipeline truce happen  
**Dr\. Stewart Prest said the deal appears to be the solution that makes the most sense, describing it as an efficient political calculation\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-ottawa-deal-massey-pipeline-9.7256802)

---

### **Department of Psychology**

**How to have a happier vacation  
**Dr\. Elizabeth Dunn said vacation happiness can begin before a trip starts, noting that anticipation, shared experiences, and planning can boost well\-being\. She also highlighted the benefits of local getaways, new experiences, and reducing phone use while travelling\.  
[The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/07/24/5-surprisingly-simple-ways-enjoy-your-vacation-more/)

**Family who lost 12\-year\-old son to cancer says ‘we are choosing to live’ by sharing in his passion  
**Dr\. Ingrid Söchting said understandings of grief have shifted away from the idea of moving through fixed stages, highlighting the concept of “continuing loving bonds” as a way people can honour loved ones while living alongside loss\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/family-son-birding-9.7268948)

**Stop shaming yourself into better habits\. Science says this emotion works better  
**Drs\. Jiaying Zhao and Elizabeth Dunn argued that positive emotions such as joy are more effective than guilt or shame for building lasting habits, including climate\-friendly behaviours, and suggested focusing on positive additions rather than restrictions\.  
[Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/kevinkruse/2026/07/08/stop-shaming-yourself-into-better-habits-science-says-this-emotion-works-better/)

---

### **Department of Sociology**

**Narcissistic leaders more likely to oppose remote work, new research suggests  
**Dr\. Sylvia Fuller said employer demands for a full return to the office may be influenced by leaders’ personal preferences and motivations, not only organizational needs, highlighting that workplace decisions are shaped by both employee and employer interests\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/study-remote-work-narcissism-9.7275176)

**Why does the World Cup feel bigger in a crowd?  
**Dr\. Neil Armitage said the World Cup’s appeal comes partly from people’s desire to come together and be part of something larger than themselves, helping explain the popularity of crowded watch parties\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/why-watching-the-world-cup-together-feels-different-9.7257233)

---

### **Department of Theatre and Film**

**Obsession becomes highest\-grossing film with budget under $1M US  
**Dr\. Ernest Mathijs said the filmmakers’ experience making short YouTube films has allowed them to refine their craft at a young age and move through the filmmaking learning curve faster than previous generations\.  
[CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment/obsession-record-box-office-400m-9.7261457)

---

### **School of Public Policy and Global Affairs**

**As Chinese economy slows, experts say there will be ‘problems for Beijing’  
**Dr\. Juliet Lu said China’s economic challenges have led consumers to become more cautious with spending, as many households have been affected by property market losses, pandemic\-era impacts, and pressures on workers from an export\-driven economy\.  
[Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/7/17/as-chinese-economy-slows-experts-say-there-will-be-problems-for-beijing)

**How the federal government’s proposed digital regulator would work  
**Dr\. Heidi Tworek said Canada’s approach to online safety regulation is unusual because the new body will oversee both privacy and online safety responsibilities, unlike some countries that separate the two functions\.  
[City News](https://vancouver.citynews.ca/2026/07/11/how-the-federal-governments-proposed-digital-regulator-would-work-2/)

---

### **Vancouver School of Economics**

**Carney looking at ‘all options’ as Trump announces 50% tariffs on Canada  
**Dr\. Michael Devereux said new tariffs targeting goods previously exempt under USMCA represent a significant escalation and signal the Trump administration’s opposition to the trade agreement it negotiated in 2018\.  
[BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cg4dzq3x3e1o)

**What happens to CUSMA on July 1? The paths ahead as review set to begin  
**Dr\. Michael Devereux said the uncertainty surrounding CUSMA highlights the need for greater stability and certainty\.  
[Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11942931/cusma-review-july-1-explained/)

---

Arts in the Media

Every month, Arts faculty share their expertise with media outlets on a variety of topics\.

**View previous instalments**

[Source link](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/?type=in-the-media)

title: Meet Dr. Steven Taubeneck: Bringing Germany closer to home
content_markdown:
*By Nick Melling*

> When Professor [Steven Taubeneck](http://cenes.ubc.ca/people/steven-taubeneck/) walked into the classroom for the first time as a teacher, he says the class just laughed\.

[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2020/04/cropped-StevenTaubeneck1.jpg)

Freshly arrived from the free\-wheeling UC Santa Cruz of the 1970s, with hair past his shoulders and a deep tan, the 28\-year\-old budding academic seemed an unlikely candidate to teach the language of Goethe and the philosophy of Kant\. “They took one look at me and thought ‘we can handle this guy,’” Taubeneck recounts\. “I laughed right along with them\.”

And his rapport with his students remains just as strong today\. Guided by the deceptively simple principle that “undergraduates should not be tortured,” he was awarded a Killam Teaching Prize in 1995, the very first year he was eligible\.

But this acclaimed teacher didn’t always see teaching as his lot in life\. “My first ambition was to be a priest,” he explains\. “Then I found about sex, so I decided I couldn’t do that\. My next ambition was to be a doctor\. Then I found out about surgery, and I knew I couldn’t do that\.”

What followed next was an 11\-year undergraduate odyssey that took him through nine different universities and six different majors, from concert piano to creative writing to Irish history\. In the end, he settled on German language and literature, which he teaches today out of the Dept\. of [Central, Eastern, and Northern European Studies](http://cenes.ubc.ca/ "Opens internal link in current window")\.

Taubeneck admits that it’s a discipline that might seem irrelevant and removed from life in Canada\. But he thinks the issues that German thinkers have long struggled with — the nature of authority, for instance, or how to deal with the past — can be applied to anyone, anywhere\. “In some ways, the Germans are ‘extremely typical,’” he explains\. “German history exhibits many of the same tendencies as the histories of other nations\.

“At the same time, there is something both horribly monstrous — Hitler — and very attractive — Bach, Mozart — about German history,” he adds\. That’s why the reading lists in Taubeneck’s classes include not only literary and philosophical classics, but also such infamous books as Hitler’s Mein Kampf\. “It’s important to read Mein Kampf in order to begin to understand the rhetoric Hitler used to attract his followers,” Taubeneck explains\. “If we can read Hitler and recognize a certain familiarity to our own times, we can better avoid similar demagogues\.”

Even his own life, Taubeneck feels, can be seen through the lens of German literature\. He says he identifies with Gregor Samsa, the main character of Franz Kafka’s Metamorphosis, who turns into a giant insect and is rejected by his family\. Born into a family whose main interests lay in the business world, Taubeneck has never felt that his parents were comfortable with career choice\. When he began reading Kafka and Nietzsche at age 11, they viewed his interest in German culture as an oddity at best, and a symptom of proto\-fascism at worst\.

But Taubeneck, who says that he went into German literature partly to fight against absolutist ideas, was unperturbed\. In his view, the passion for one’s field of study is exactly what makes a good teacher\.

“Professors are really just older children who have followed their obsessions to the point of making careers out of them,” he observes\. “Aren’t they?”

Students who share Taubeneck’s obsessions can join him in one of five upper\-level classes\. Topics range from wartime literature and European politics to communism and existentialism\.

title: Your guide to UBC Arts scholarships and awards
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2021/03/22656500348_bc2158ea7f_o.png)

> Hundreds of scholarships and awards are available at UBC\. Here’s where to start, who can help, and how to find the ones you’re eligible for\.

---

### **Where should I start?**

-   **The Arts funding page\.** This is your best first stop\. It shares specific awards for Arts students, along with eligibility, requirements and deadlines for each\.
-   **Your department website\.** Music, Asian Studies, Theatre & Film… whatever your major/minor is, check there next\.
    -   If you’re doing [GoGlobal](https://goglobal.ubc.ca/go-global/programs-ubc-students), [Arts Co\-op](https://artscoop.ubc.ca/) or a club, check out those sites too\. Some have awards you’d never stumble on otherwise\!
-   **UBC\-wide options\.** Once you’ve covered your bases in Arts, search the [UBC Awards](https://students.ubc.ca/finances/awards-scholarships-bursaries/) site, and the [UBC Award Search Database](https://tools.students.ubc.ca/award-search/) to find what’s open to everyone\.
-   **Google it\.** Use your own specific interests and strengths to find something tailored to you\. Olivia Stedman \(BA’22\) built her whole list this way: “I would Google the exact words of the scholarship that I wanted, searching with terms like ‘Canadian student’ or ‘volunteered abroad’ or ‘working from a young age, etc\.’”

### **💡 TIP**

Apply early\! Most Arts award deadlines are early in the fall \(October/November\)\.

Find scholarships & awards for Arts students

*arrow\_right\_alt*

[Source link](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/student-support/funding/)

---

### **What’s the difference between an award, a scholarship, a prize, and a bursary?**

These words are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things when it comes to actually applying\.

-   **Award:** this is based on your lived experience, not just your transcript\. Leadership, volunteering, etc\. You’ll also hear “award” used loosely as a catch\-all term for any of the four types of funding\.
-   **Scholarship:** based purely on your academic achievements\. The good news is that some of these are automatic, and tied straight to your grades\.
-   **Prize:** given if you’re the top student in a specific class\. Usually, no application is required\.
-   **Bursary:** a non\-repayable, need\-based award\. This fills the gap between your student loans and what you still need, if you’re a domestic student\.

---

### **How long does an application take? How many scholarships and awards should I apply for?**

-   Set aside about **an hour and a half** per application \(but that’s just an average\)\. Matthias Leuprecht \(BIE’22\) says some took him as little as half an hour, others closer to 10 hours\. It really depends on the award\.
-   Start with 3 to 5 awards\. Apply for what you’re eligible for now, then widen your search as you get more comfortable with the process\. Targeting your applications also makes them stronger\. As Olivia puts it: “\[Targeting specific scholarships\] makes your answers to the essay questions so much more in depth\.”

### **💡 TIP**

Don’t skip the niche awards just because they seem oddly specific\. Fewer people apply, so your odds are often better\.

---

### **What goes in my application?**

The main thing is to talk about what you learned, how you learned it, and what you’ll take from it going forward\. Beyond that, a few things that make a real difference:

-   **Answer every question\.** Don’t leave anything half\-finished, even the ones that feel optional\.
-   **Connect the dots\.** Draw a clear line between your own experience and what the award is actually looking for\.
-   **Be honest\.** Vulnerability goes a long way\. Adjudication committees are people too, and they respond to a real story more than a polished one\.

The strength of your application comes down to the time and effort you put into it\. Rushed answers tend to read that way\.

---

### **Who can help me with my application?**

-   Start with your [Enrolment Services Advisor](https://students.ubc.ca/about-student-services/enrolment-services-advisors/)\. They’re your first point of contact for any questions about awards and scholarships, big and small\.
-   If your question is specific to something the Faculty of Arts offers, the [Dean of Arts Office](mailto:arts.awards@ubc.ca) can help too\.

---

Start your search 🔍

Find scholarships and awards for Arts students\.

**Start here**

title: Need an elective? Try one of these hidden gems 💎
content_markdown:
[Image](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/08/hiddengems-header_v2.jpg)

> Still need an elective for Winter Term 1? We’ve done some digging 👀

We’ve rounded up some hidden gems from across Arts, from language, literature and performance to politics, history and life’s big questions\. Take a look, find something that sparks your curiosity and add it to your timetable\.

---

Expand all

\|

Collapse all

[Language, literature and performance \(12\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/hidden-gems-winter-term-1-2026/#language-literature-and-perfor-40)

[**LING\_V 101: Languages of the World**](https://linguistics.ubc.ca/undergraduate/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=LING%20101)  
Trace how the world's thousands of languages are classified, evolve, and sometimes disappear, from writing systems to endangered languages\.  
*Multiple sections\. Offered both WT1 and WT2\.*

---

[**MUSC 165B/466B/565B: World Music Ensembles**](https://music.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=165B)  
Play Balinese gamelan instruments in a performance ensemble, no music reading or prior experience required, building toward an end\-of\-year concert\.  
*Wed/Fri, 1:00 PM–2:50 PM\. Full\-year course, both terms required\.*

---

[**SWAH\_V 101: Beginners Swahili I**](https://africanstudies.arts.ubc.ca/courses-2/2026-winter/)  
Start speaking Swahili, one of the world's most widely spoken languages, through everyday vocabulary and real cultural context\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM*

---

[**ASIA\_V 212: Writing about Japan**](https://asia.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=Writing%20about%20Japan%20212)  
Read everything from ancient myths to travel narratives to the "Cool Japan" phenomenon, and see how Japan has been imagined and re\-imagined across centuries through literature and pop culture\.  
*Tue/Thu, 12:30 PM–2:00 PM*

---

[**RMST\_V 201: Intro to Literatures and Cultures of the Romance World I**](https://fhis.ubc.ca/course-description/rmst201/)  
Read *Don Quixote*, *Dante's Inferno*, and *Madame Bovary* in translation, and trace 500 years of literary history across France, Spain, Portugal, and Italy\.  
*Tue/Thu, 12:30 PM–2:00 PM*

---

[**AMNE\_V 392: Introduction to Akkadian**](https://wd10.myworkday.com/ubc/d/inst/3$49941/13228$477174.htmld#TABTASKID=2998%2426057)  
Learn Akkadian, the language of the world's oldest surviving written story, and explore everything from royal epics and divine myths to treaties, oaths, and adoption contracts\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 2:00 PM–3:00 PM*

---

[**ASIA\_V 357: Modern Korean Literature in Translation**](https://asia.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=ASIA%20357%20011)  
Discover Korea's modern history through fiction on gender, division, trauma, and LGBTQ experiences, no Korean language required\.  
*Mon/Wed, 3:30 PM–5:00 PM*

---

[**GMST\_V 341: Nineteenth\-Century German Literature and Social Media**](https://cenes.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=GMST%20341)  
Dig into 19th\-century scandals, fake news, and periodical press in German\-speaking Europe, and see how familiar the media chaos feels today\.  
*Mon/Wed, 12:30 PM–2:00 PM*

---

[**NORD\_V 334: Resilient Narratives: Anxiety and Grief in Contemporary Nordic Fiction**](https://cenes.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=334)  
Explore grief, anxiety, and the occasional scary troll through contemporary Nordic fiction and children's literature\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM*

---

[**THTR 340B: Studies in Asian Theatre**](https://theatrefilm.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=THTR%20340)  
Explore how modern theatre took shape across Asia, from colonial influence and nationalism to reforming existing theatrical traditions, through plays from China, Japan, India, Indonesia, Korea, and Vietnam\.  
*Mon/Wed, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---

[**ASIA\_V 412: Pre\-Modern Chinese Poetry**](https://asia.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=ASIA%20412)  
Read early Chinese poetry by Qu Yuan, Cao Cao, and Tao Yuanming, plus anonymous voices, in translation, and build the tools to make sense of texts written centuries ago\.  
*Mon/Wed, 11:00 AM–12:30 PM*

---

[**FNEL 489A: Language, Landscape, and All Our Relations**](https://cis.arts.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=489A)  
Explore how ancestral languages and landscapes are inseparable, and what it means to document and reclaim a language through land\.  
*Mon/Wed, 11:00 AM–12:30 PM*

[Politics, History, and Ethics \(16\)](https://www.arts.ubc.ca/news/hidden-gems-winter-term-1-2026/#politics-history-and-ethics-16-41)

[**ANTH\_V 275: Anthropology of Migration and \(Im\)mobilities**](https://anth.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=ANTH%20275)  
Examine the lived, everyday realities of migration and border\-crossing, and the forces that constrain who gets to move freely\.  
*Tue/Thu, 9:30 AM–11:00 AM*

---

[**CENS\_V 201 \(Sec 101\): Controlling Objects**](https://cenes.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=Contrasts%20and%20Conflicts)  
Unpack how your phone, your clothes, and your commute quietly shape who you are, through a century of literature, film, and photography\.  
*Tue/Thu, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---

[**CENS\_V 201 \(Sec 103\): Ukraine: Narratives We Didn't Know**](https://cenes.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=Contrasts%20and%20Conflicts)  
Trace Ukraine's story from the twentieth century to today through literature and film you probably haven't encountered yet\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM*

---

[**CSIS\_V 200: Introduction to Critical Studies in Gender and Sexuality**](https://grsj.arts.ubc.ca/courses/)  
Build a foundation in sexuality studies, and see how sexuality intersects with race, class, ability, and power rather than existing on its own\.  
*Tue/Thu, 11:00 AM–12:30 PM*

---

[**FNIS\_V 210: Indigenous Politics and Self\-Determination**](https://cis.arts.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=210)  
Get into the politics, land claims, and self\-government struggles that define the relationship between Indigenous peoples and the Canadian government\.  
*Mon/Wed, 9:30 AM–11:00 AM*

---

[**HIST 217: Global History Before 1500: Eurasia**](https://history.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=217)  
Rewrite your mental map of the ancient world, from Sumer to the Caliphate, without Europe at the centre\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM*

---

[**PHIL\_V 222: Enriched Symbolic Logic**](https://philosophy.ubc.ca/courses/)  
Build formal proofs from the ground up, from set theory to predicate logic, if you like puzzles with actual right answers\.  
*Mon/Wed, 11:00 AM–12:30 PM*

---

[**PHIL\_V 230: Introduction to Ethics**](https://philosophy.ubc.ca/courses/)  
Wrestle with what actually makes something right or wrong, through classic and contemporary readings on obligation and value\.  
*Mon/Wed, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM*

---

[**PSYC\_V 203: Career Exploration Using Psychology**](https://psych.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=PSYC%20203)  
Apply psychology to your own career planning, with real strategies for figuring out what's next, not just theory about other people\.  
*Sec 002: Mon, 2:00 PM–3:00 PM\. Sec 003: Mon, 3:00 PM–4:00 PM*

---

[**AMNE\_V 318: The Roman Republic**](https://wd10.myworkday.com/ubc/d/inst/3$49941/13228$477174.htmld#TABTASKID=2998%2426057)  
Follow Rome from its founding through the collapse of the Republic, and see how empire\-building and political dysfunction fed each other\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 2:00 PM–3:00 PM*

---

[**AMNE\_V 361: The Origins of Judaism**](https://wd10.myworkday.com/ubc/d/inst/3$49941/13228$477119.htmld#TABTASKID=2998%2426057)  
Trace the history of Jews and Judaism from the destruction of the First Temple to the roots of the rabbinic tradition\.  
*Mon/Wed/Fri, 10:00 AM–11:00 AM*

---

[**ASIA\_V 366: Queer/Early/Asias**](https://asia.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=ASIA%20366C)  
Dig into queer life across pre\-modern Asia through texts, field trips, and film screenings, and help re\-imagine queer Asian futures\.  
*Tue/Thu, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---

[**ASIA\_V 373: History of Hong Kong**](https://hksi.ubc.ca/asia-hist-373/)  
Trace Hong Kong's transformation from a 19th\-century colonial port to one of the world's most distinct global cities\.  
*Mon/Wed, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---

[**ASIX\_V 300: News, Information, and Knowledge in Early Modern East Asia**](https://asia.ubc.ca/courses/?academic-period=2026w&search=ASIX%20300V)  
See how "fake news" anxieties played out across Ming China, Tokugawa Japan, and Joseon Korea centuries before social media\.  
*Mon, 11:00 AM–12:00 PM / Wed, 11:00 AM–1:00 PM*

---

[**LAST\_V 315A: Food in Mexico and Central America**](https://las.arts.ubc.ca/last-315/)  
Study corn, cuisine, and identity in Mexico and Central America, from pre\-colonial cosmologies to the politics of your dinner plate today\.  
*Mon/Wed, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---

[**ASIX\_V 430: Indigenous Environmentalism in Asia**](https://scarp.ubc.ca/news/2026/new-course-generative-ai-cities-and-society)  
Explore how Indigenous environmentalism is embodied, experienced, and expressed across Asia and beyond, beginning with the xʷməθkʷəy̓əm land where the course is taught\.  
*Tue, 2:00 PM–3:30 PM*

---
